The agency acknowledges each complaint within 2 business days and works to resolve it within 14 days. These two periods are agency policy and are not set by rule. Clients are told they may also contact their case management agency, ODA or ODM about services, and ODH about licensure concerns. Every complaint and its outcome is logged. Complaints involving suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation are handled under SAF-01 and are not delayed by this process.

definitions.definition: Any expression of dissatisfaction about services, staff, billing, scheduling or rights, whether or not the client uses the word complaint.
Any adverse action such as reduced services, schedule changes, threats or harsher treatment because someone complained.
Monday through Friday, except legal holidays.

procedures: At intake, the staff member explains the complaint process and gives the client a written notice in plain language, in the client's preferred language or format, stating how to complain (by phone at [PHONE], in writing to [ADDRESS], through the caregiver or supervisor, or through a representative).

The notice states that complaining will not affect services, and lists outside contacts: the case management agency, ODA at 1-800-266-4346, ODM Integrated Help Desk at 1-800-686-1516, and ODH (home health licensure page at odh.ohio.gov) for licensure concerns. Receiving help from the agency does not limit the client's right to contact outside agencies.
Any staff member who receives a complaint writes down who complained, when, what was said, and what was asked for, and gives it to the Administrator or supervisor the same business day.
The Administrator enters the complaint in the Complaint Log with a number, date received and category.
If the complaint alleges abuse, neglect, exploitation, theft or injury, the Administrator starts SAF-01 or SAF-02 immediately and also logs the complaint here.
The Administrator or supervisor acknowledges the complaint to the complainant, orally or in writing, within 2 business days, and explains who will look into it and the 14-day target.

A person not involved in the events investigates. The investigator talks with the complainant, relevant staff and, where needed, the case management agency, and reviews the service plan, schedules, EVV records (SVC-09) and visit notes.

Staff named in a complaint are not scheduled to handle it and are told not to retaliate. If safety could be at risk, the Administrator changes the caregiver assignment while the matter is reviewed (SVC-07).

The Administrator decides on the resolution and tells the complainant of the outcome, in the complainant's preferred format, within 14 days of receipt. If the complaint cannot be resolved in 14 days, the Administrator tells the complainant why, gives a new date in writing, and repeats the update at least every 7 days.
The written outcome describes what was found, what the agency will do, and the complainant's right to take the complaint to the case management agency, ODA, ODM or ODH if not satisfied.
If the complainant remains dissatisfied, the Administrator offers a meeting with the governing body representative and records the result.
If the complaint involves a Medicaid-funded service and affects service delivery or eligibility, the Administrator notifies the case management agency or payer (SVC-12, SVC-14).

The Administrator closes the log entry with the outcome, the date of response and any corrective action, and files the complaint record separately from the personnel file but cross-referenced to it if staff discipline occurred (PER-13).
The Administrator summarizes complaints by type, caregiver and outcome each quarter for the governing body (GOV-05) and uses patterns to change training or procedures.

responsibilities.duty: Own the process, assign investigators, meet the 2-business-day and 14-day periods, and prevent retaliation.
Take complaints, acknowledge them and assist with investigation.
Take any complaint seriously, pass it on the same business day and never retaliate.
Review complaint trends and hear unresolved complaints.

documentation: Complaint Log with dates received, acknowledged and resolved
Written complaint notice given at intake
Investigation notes and outcome letters
Corrective action records
Quarterly complaint summary

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All employees, volunteers, contractors and the governing body
policies.purpose: To protect the privacy of client information and agency records and to meet state and federal confidentiality laws.
policies.policy: This policy meets OAC 173-39-02(B)(4) (Confidentiality). [AGENCY NAME] is subject to state and federal confidentiality laws, including ORC 5160.45 to 5160.481, 42 CFR 431.300 to 431.307, and 45 CFR parts 160, 162 and 164, and complies with them. The agency also complies with HIPAA and 42 CFR 431 as a Medicaid waiver provider (OAC 5160-44-31). Criminal records check reports are confidential and are kept apart from general personnel files (ORC 3740.11). Staff may not post photos or information about clients on social media without the client's written consent. Client information is released only with a written authorization from the client or as the law permits.

definitions.definition: Individually identifiable information about a client's health, care or payment, in any form, held by the agency.
A written, signed permission from the client or legal representative that names what may be released, to whom and for how long.
An unauthorized acquisition, access, use or disclosure of PHI that compromises its security or privacy.

procedures: The Administrator serves as Privacy Officer unless the governing body names another person in writing. The name and [PHONE] are included in the Notice of Privacy Practices.

At intake, the staff member gives the client the Notice of Privacy Practices, explains how information is used and shared (for care, payment and operations), and obtains a signed acknowledgment (CR-01).
Every employee, volunteer and contractor signs a confidentiality agreement at hire and annually, and is trained on this policy at orientation and in annual in-service (PER-09, PER-11).
Staff access only the client information needed for their job. Caregivers see only their assigned clients' plans.
Staff do not discuss clients in public places, with other clients or with family not listed in the record. They do not leave records, phones or tablets unattended in vehicles or homes.
Records are kept in locked storage at the business site and in password-protected systems with individual log-ins, and are available to ODA, ODM, HHS and the Auditor as required (REC-03).

Client information is released only: (a) with a signed authorization; (b) to the case management agency, payers, ODH, ODA, ODM or other regulators as permitted by law; or (c) in an emergency to protect health or safety. Each release is logged.

Photos, video or posts about a client on social media or elsewhere are prohibited unless the client or legal representative gives written consent in advance. Staff may not photograph clients or their homes with personal phones for any other reason.

Criminal records check reports and related applicant information are kept in a separate locked file and shared only with persons who need them to make the hiring decision or with regulators (PER-04, PER-13).
Staff who lose a device or record, or who see an improper disclosure, report it to the Privacy Officer the same day.

The Privacy Officer investigates, limits harm, notifies the client without unreasonable delay, and decides whether notification of HHS or others is required under 45 CFR Part 164. The Privacy Officer documents the finding and corrective steps in the incident file (SAF-02).
Clients may ask to see, correct, or receive a copy of their records, and may request an accounting of disclosures. The Privacy Officer responds in writing and within the time that law allows.
Violation of this policy is grounds for discipline up to termination (PER-15). No staff member is retaliated against for reporting a privacy concern.
The Privacy Officer reviews this policy, security practices and the disclosure log each year (GOV-04) and when laws change.

responsibilities.duty: Enforce the policy, train staff, handle releases, requests and breaches.
Make sure caregivers protect records and devices and report concerns.
Use only the information needed, keep it secure, obtain consent before any social media use, and report incidents the same day.

documentation: Notice of Privacy Practices and signed client acknowledgments
Signed staff confidentiality agreements and training records
Authorization forms and the disclosure log
Social media consent forms
Breach and incident investigation records
Separate confidential file for criminal records check reports

policies.title: Client Property, Gifts and Financial Exploitation Prevention
policies.applies_to: All employees, volunteers and contractors
policies.purpose: To protect clients from financial exploitation and to keep staff conduct with client property and money professional and transparent.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] prohibits staff from accepting gifts, tips, loans or purchases from clients and from selling goods or services to, or buying from, clients (OAC 173-39-02(B); OAC 5160-44-31). Staff may not use a client's food, supplies or other property for themselves and may not act as a client's power of attorney or guardian. Staff may handle client money only as stated in the written service plan and with receipts. Staff must not falsify signatures or records. Suspected exploitation is reported under SAF-01. Whether a relative may be paid as a caregiver follows the applicable ODM rule for Medicaid programs, which the Administrator verifies before any relative is hired or billed.

definitions.definition: Money, tips, items, services or favors of any value given to a staff member by a client or family because of the care relationship.
Any improper use of a client's money, property or assets, including theft, coercion, misuse of accounts or cards, or persuading a client to give or lend.
A shopping or similar task listed in the written service plan in which a caregiver handles client money, with receipts and a record.

procedures: At hire and annually, every staff member signs the Conduct and Property statement acknowledging the rules in steps 2-6 and the discipline for violations (PER-15).

Staff may not accept gifts, tips, loans or purchases from clients or family. If a client offers a gift, the staff member politely declines, explains the agency rule, and tells the supervisor the same day. Perishable items of nominal value shared by the whole household may be left in the home but are never taken.
Staff may not sell products, services, raffle tickets or fundraising items to clients, nor buy from clients, borrow from them, or lend them money.

Staff may not use a client's food, supplies, telephone, vehicle, computer or other property for personal use. They may not take items from the home, other than items the client directs be thrown away as trash in the service plan.

Staff may not act as a client's power of attorney, guardian, representative payee or other legal decision-maker, may not be named in a client's will or beneficiary designation, and may not help a client change a will or account.

Staff may not handle client money, cards, checks or PINs, except for authorized errands listed in the service plan. The supervisor writes the authorization into the plan with the client's signed consent, and sets a spending limit.

For an authorized errand, the caregiver counts the money with the client before and after, keeps the receipt, returns the change and the receipt to the client, and the client signs the Errand Log. The caregiver never uses the client's card for personal needs and never keeps the card or PIN.
Staff may not falsify any client signature, timesheet, EVV entry or service record, and may not bill for time when the client is hospitalized or services were not delivered (SVC-09).
At intake, the staff member tells the client and family of these rules and gives the Loss Claim Instructions (GOV-08).

A caregiver who notices missing money or property, unusual bills or checks, pressure from others on the client, or changes in the client's will or accounts reports it to the supervisor the same day. The caregiver does not confront the client or a suspect.

The supervisor tells the Administrator the same day. The Administrator reports suspected exploitation under SAF-01, opens an incident report under SAF-02, and notifies the case management agency (SVC-14).
The Administrator immediately removes a caregiver from the home if he or she is alleged to have taken, borrowed, or used client property, pending the outcome.
The supervisor reviews Errand Logs and receipts at each supervisory visit (SVC-04) and compares them to the service plan.

Before any relative of a client is hired or paid to provide care, the Administrator confirms eligibility under the applicable ODM rule and the payer's requirements, and documents the decision. The agency does not bill for any relative whose eligibility has not been confirmed.
The Administrator reviews violations and corrective actions at least yearly in the quality program (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Enforce the rules, remove staff when needed, report exploitation and verify relative eligibility.
Authorize errands in the plan, audit Errand Logs and receipts and handle same-day reports.
Decline gifts and loans, protect client property, keep receipts and report any concern.
Understand that staff cannot accept gifts or handle money beyond the plan and report concerns.

documentation: Signed Conduct and Property statements
Service plans authorizing errands, and Errand Logs with receipts
Incident and exploitation reports
Gift offer reports
Relative-eligibility determinations
Disciplinary records

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Language Access
policies.applies_to: All employees, caregivers, supervisors and contractors of [AGENCY NAME]; all applicants, clients and their representatives, whether private-pay, PASSPORT or Ohio Home Care Waiver.
policies.purpose: To make sure every person who asks for or receives services from [AGENCY NAME] is treated without discrimination. This includes people with limited English proficiency (LEP) and people with disabilities, who must be able to understand and use our plans, notices and services at no cost to them.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not refuse, limit or end services, and does not treat any person differently, because of race, color, national origin, disability, age, sex or religion. As an ODA-certified agency we attest compliance with 45 CFR 80.4 and with equal employment opportunity laws (OAC 173-39-02(C)(1)), and we comply with the Americans with Disabilities Act (42 USC 12101). Service plans and notices must be accessible to people with limited English proficiency and to people with disabilities (OAC 5160-44-02). Interpreter and translation help is provided at no cost to the client. We may decline a referral only for a non-discriminatory reason, such as needs outside the nonmedical scope (SVC-01), no authorization, or inadequate staffing (SVC-02). That reason is documented. This policy applies equally to hiring and employment decisions.

definitions.definition: A person who does not speak English as a primary language and has a limited ability to read, speak, write or understand English.
A change in how a service, notice or process is provided so that a person with a disability can take part equally, without undue burden on the agency.
A qualified person who orally conveys information between English and another language, including sign language.
A written version of a document in another language or in an accessible format (for example large print, Braille or plain-language read-aloud).

procedures: The Administrator, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], is the nondiscrimination coordinator and can be reached at [PHONE]. This contact is listed in the client handbook and on the nondiscrimination notice.

At the first contact and at intake, the intake coordinator asks every applicant for their preferred spoken and written language, whether they need an interpreter, and whether they need any accessibility accommodation (for example hearing, vision, mobility or reading support). The answers are recorded on the intake form.

The intake coordinator gives each applicant the nondiscrimination notice and the client rights statement (CR-01) in the applicant's preferred language or accessible format. The notice states that interpreter and translation help is free and explains how to file a complaint under CR-02.

When a client or representative needs language help, the Administrator arranges a qualified interpreter (in person, by telephone or by video) before the visit or meeting. The agency pays all costs, and the client is never billed.

Caregivers and supervisors do not require a client to use a family member or friend as interpreter. A family member may interpret only if the client asks for that, and this request is documented. Minors are not used as interpreters except in an emergency.

The supervisor makes sure the service plan, the service agreement (CR-06), grievance information and any notice of change or discharge are provided in plain language and in the client's preferred language or accessible format, consistent with OAC 5160-44-02. Translated or alternate-format documents are signed and distributed as the English versions are.

When a document cannot be translated before it is needed, the supervisor goes through it with the client using an interpreter, documents that this was done, and provides the written translation as soon as it is available.

The Administrator reviews each accommodation request within [NUMBER] business days, grants it unless it would fundamentally change the service or create an undue burden, and documents the decision. If an accommodation cannot be provided, the Administrator offers an effective alternative and documents it.

Staff are trained on this policy at orientation (PER-09) and in annual in-service (PER-11). The training covers how to arrange an interpreter, respectful communication with people with disabilities, and the ban on discrimination.

Caregivers must report to the supervisor at once any request for language or accessibility help that they cannot meet. They must never ignore the request or let a client go without a needed service because of a language or disability barrier.

Any decision to decline or end services is reviewed by the Administrator before it is made. The reason is written on the decision record. Reasons based on a protected characteristic are never allowed.

Complaints of discrimination are handled under CR-02 without retaliation. The Administrator logs the complaint, investigates, and gives the complainant a written response within the time stated in CR-02.

The Administrator keeps current the agency's attestations of compliance with 45 CFR 80.4, equal employment opportunity, wage-hour and workers' compensation laws, as submitted to ODA (OAC 173-39-02(C)(1)). Any substantiated discrimination finding is reported to the governing body and addressed in the QAPI review (GOV-05).
Each year the Administrator reviews the language of clients served, interpreter use, accommodation requests and complaints, and updates this policy and the list of available interpreter resources.

responsibilities.duty: Serves as nondiscrimination coordinator, arranges interpreters and translation, decides accommodation requests, investigates discrimination complaints and keeps ODA attestations current.
Asks about language and accessibility needs at first contact, records them, and gives the nondiscrimination notice.
Makes sure plans, agreements and notices reach the client in a usable language and format, and uses an interpreter for visits and plan reviews.
Treat every client with respect, never discriminate, and tell the supervisor right away about any language or accessibility barrier.
Reviews annual nondiscrimination and language access reports and supports resources for interpreters and translation.

documentation: Language and accessibility needs on the intake form
Signed acknowledgment of the nondiscrimination notice
Interpreter and translation request log (date, language, interpreter name or service, who requested)
Accommodation request and decision records
Records of any decision to decline or end services, with the non-discriminatory reason
Discrimination complaint log and investigation files (see CR-02)
Staff training sign-in sheets
Current attestations submitted to ODA

policies.title: Service Agreement, Rates and Billing Disclosure
policies.applies_to: Intake staff, billing staff, supervisors and the Administrator; all private-pay, PASSPORT and Ohio Home Care Waiver clients.
policies.purpose: To make sure every client knows, in writing and before services start, what services will be provided, what they will cost (if anything), and how billing and ending of services work, and to protect Medicaid and ODA clients from being charged beyond the agreed rate.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] gives each client a written service agreement before services begin. For private-pay clients, the agreement states the hourly rate, the minimum visit length, cancellation terms, the billing cycle, the scope of services, and that caregivers do not administer medications. For Medicaid and ODA-funded clients, the agency accepts the agreed rate as payment in full and never balance-bills the client (OAC 173-39-02(B)). The agreement is written in plain language and is accessible to the client in their language and format (OAC 5160-44-02; see CR-05). The agency gives the 30-day notice of service end described in SVC-11. The client receives a copy, and the signed original is kept in the client record.

definitions.definition: The written contract between [AGENCY NAME] and the client (or representative) describing services, rates, billing and the rights and duties of each party.
Charging a client for any part of the cost of an authorized, Medicaid- or ODA-paid service beyond the agreed rate.
The rate that the agency has agreed to accept from ODA, ODM or the managed program as full payment for an authorized service.
A client who pays [AGENCY NAME] directly rather than through PASSPORT, the Ohio Home Care Waiver or other payer.

procedures: Before the first visit, the intake coordinator reviews the service agreement with the client or representative, with an interpreter or accessible format when needed (CR-05), and answers questions. The agreement is not signed until the client says they understand it.

For private-pay clients, the agreement lists: the hourly rate of [HOURLY RATE]; the minimum visit length of [MINIMUM VISIT LENGTH]; the cancellation terms ([CANCELLATION NOTICE AND ANY CHARGE]); the billing cycle and due date ([BILLING CYCLE]); accepted payment methods; and any charge for late payment, if used.

The private-pay agreement describes the scope of services in plain terms, consistent with SVC-01 and the service plan (SVC-03). It states that caregivers do not administer medications, and that they only remind, hand over or open containers, or assist with self-administration as allowed.
The private-pay agreement states how and when the rate may change. Rate changes require [NUMBER] days' written notice to the client before the change takes effect.

For PASSPORT and Ohio Home Care Waiver clients, the agreement states the services and hours authorized by the program, that the agency accepts the program rate as payment in full, and that the client owes the agency nothing for authorized services (OAC 173-39-02(B)). Billing staff never send a bill, statement or collection notice to these clients for authorized services.

If a Medicaid or ODA client asks for services in addition to the authorized hours, the supervisor first refers the client to their case manager to ask for an authorization change. Services outside the authorization may be provided only under a separate, voluntary private-pay agreement that the client signs, that shows the rate, and that does not replace or reduce authorized services. The Administrator approves each such agreement before services start.
The agreement includes the agency's process for ending services, including the 30-day notice requirement in SVC-11, and the client's right to end services at any time.
The agreement includes how to file a grievance (CR-02), the client rights statement (CR-01), and the agency phone number [PHONE] and address [ADDRESS].

The client or representative signs and dates the agreement, and an agency representative signs it. The intake coordinator gives the client a complete copy on the day of signing and records the date given.
The signed original is placed in the client record the same day (REC-01). If the client cannot sign, the reason and the name of the person who signed on their behalf are documented.
Billing staff issue private-pay invoices on the billing cycle in the agreement. Each invoice lists dates, hours and rate, and agrees with the hours verified through visit records (SVC-09).
Billing staff review billing monthly for Medicaid and ODA clients to make sure the agency bills only for authorized, delivered and verified services. Any overpayment found is corrected under GOV-06.
The supervisor reviews the agreement with the client whenever the service plan changes significantly (SVC-03). Any amendment is in writing, signed and copied as above.
Billing and service records are kept for 6 years after payment, or until any review or audit ends if later (OAC 173-39-02(B); REC-01).
The Administrator reviews the agreement template each year, and whenever rules or rates change, under GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Reviews the agreement with the client, obtains signatures, gives the client a copy and files the original.
Bill only the agreed rate, never balance-bill Medicaid or ODA clients, and match invoices to verified visits.
Refers requests for added hours to the case manager and reviews the agreement when the plan changes.
Approves the agreement template and any additional private-pay agreement, and resolves billing disputes.

documentation: Signed service agreement with the date a copy was given to the client
Private-pay rate sheet and notices of rate change
Separate private-pay agreements for any services beyond authorization, with Administrator approval
Invoices and payment records
Billing-to-visit reconciliation
Notices of service end (see SVC-11)
Billing records retained 6 years after payment, or until any review or audit ends

policies.title: Scope of Services - What Caregivers May and May Not Do
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, PCA supervisors, intake staff and the Administrator.
policies.purpose: To define clearly the nonmedical services that [AGENCY NAME] provides, and the tasks that caregivers must not perform, so clients are safe and the agency stays within its ODH nonmedical license and Medicaid program rules.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides nonmedical home health services as defined in ORC 3740.01 and OAC 3701-60-01. These are home health aide services and personal care services, including help with self-administration of medication. Caregivers may provide hands-on help with activities of daily living (ADLs) and instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs), home management, homemaker tasks and errands, and help with self-administration of medication, as authorized in the service plan (OAC 173-39-02.11). Caregivers do not perform nursing or skilled tasks and do not administer prescribed or over-the-counter medication (OAC 5160-46-04). Caregivers do only the tasks in the service plan, within the authorized hours. Respite is excluded from ODA personal care (OAC 173-39-02.11(A)). Job descriptions mirror this scope (PER-03).

definitions.definition: Hands-on and supportive services such as bathing, dressing, grooming, toileting, mobility and transfers, eating help, and IADL support, as defined in OAC 3701-60-01 and OAC 173-39-02.11.
Activities of daily living (such as bathing, dressing, toileting, eating, mobility) and instrumental activities of daily living (such as meal preparation, housekeeping, laundry, shopping, errands).

Reminding the client to take medication, handing the client the container, opening the container, and assisting a physically impaired client, as listed in OAC 3701-60-01(Y) and OAC 5160-46-04. The client decides to take, and takes, their own medication.
Any task that requires a licensed nurse's judgment or training, such as injections, wound care, sterile procedures, or assessing and treating a condition.
Short-term relief for a family caregiver. It is excluded from ODA personal care under OAC 173-39-02.11(A) and is not provided under that service.

procedures: Before services start, the PCA supervisor lists in the service plan (SVC-03) each task the caregiver will do and the authorized hours. Caregivers receive a copy of the task list for their assigned client.

Allowed tasks include: bathing, dressing, grooming and skin care of the intact skin type taught in orientation; toileting and incontinence care; mobility, positioning and transfers as set out in the plan; help with eating; meal preparation; light housekeeping and laundry; shopping and errands as authorized; and companionship during other tasks.

Help with medication is limited to reminding, handing the container to the client, opening the container, and assisting a physically impaired client (OAC 3701-60-01(Y); OAC 5160-46-04). Details are in SVC-06.

Caregivers must not give, pour, measure, place in the mouth, inject or otherwise administer any prescribed or over-the-counter medication, and must not decide when or how much medication a client takes.

Caregivers must not perform nursing or other skilled tasks. If a client needs one, the caregiver does not perform it and calls the supervisor at once. The supervisor screens the need under SVC-02 and refers it to the client's physician, case manager or a licensed home health provider.
Caregivers perform only tasks in the current plan, within the authorized hours (OAC 5160-46-04). They do not work extra hours or add tasks on their own initiative.

If a client or family member asks a caregiver to do a task that is not on the plan, the caregiver politely declines, explains that they must check first, and calls the supervisor the same day. The supervisor decides whether the task is allowed, refers a plan change under SVC-03, and documents the decision.
Respite is not provided as an ODA personal care service. If a family asks for respite, the supervisor explains the limit and refers the family to the case manager for other options.
If a caregiver is uncertain whether a task is allowed, the caregiver does not perform it and asks the supervisor. No caregiver is disciplined for declining a task they believe is outside scope.

A caregiver who is asked, pressured or directed to perform an out-of-scope task by a client, family member or agency staff reports it to the Administrator, and the matter is handled under SAF-02 and PER-15. Retaliation is prohibited.
Supervisors observe task performance at each supervisory visit (SVC-04) and note any scope concern. Out-of-scope performance is corrected with the caregiver in writing and may result in discipline.

The Administrator confirms every year that this policy, the client agreement (CR-06), the service plan template and job descriptions (PER-03) all match the current scope under ORC 3740.01 and the rules cited above.
Where the Ohio Home Care Waiver aide requirements differ from ODA personal care, SVC-13 is followed in addition to this policy.

responsibilities.duty: Perform only tasks in the plan within authorized hours, never administer medication or do nursing tasks, and call the supervisor with any doubt.
Defines tasks in the plan, answers scope questions, observes practice and corrects violations.
Screens out and refers needs outside the nonmedical scope before accepting a referral.
Keeps the scope, job descriptions and agreements consistent and investigates scope violations.

documentation: Service plan with task list and authorized hours
Supervisor's record of scope questions and decisions
Referral records for needs outside scope
Observation notes from supervisory visits
Corrective action records
Annual scope review record

policies.title: Client Intake, Eligibility and Assessment
policies.applies_to: Intake coordinator, PCA supervisors (RN or LPN), scheduler and the Administrator.
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] accepts only clients whose needs are within the nonmedical scope, who are properly enrolled and authorized when payment is through Medicaid or PASSPORT, and for whom the agency has adequate caregiver and supervisor staffing before services begin.
policies.policy: This policy meets OAC 173-39-02.11(C)(2)(a), Availability and staffing: [AGENCY NAME] accepts a referral only if there are adequate staffing levels of PCAs and PCA supervisors to provide the hours authorized for each individual (OAC 173-39-02.11(C)(2)). The staffing check is documented on the intake form. A PCA supervisor completes an in-home assessment before or at the first service episode. Medicaid and PASSPORT clients must be enrolled and authorized, and for PASSPORT an open enrollment slot is required (OAC 5160-31-03). The agency accepts referrals only for enrolled, authorized individuals. Needs that are outside the nonmedical scope are screened out and referred elsewhere. Planning follows the person-centered principles of OAC 5160-44-02. The individual leads the planning and the information is provided in an accessible way.

definitions.definition: A request for services from a client, family, case management agency, Area Agency on Aging/Council on Aging or other source.
The service, number of hours and period approved by the payer or case manager for the individual.
Enough qualified PCAs, and enough RN or LPN supervisor capacity, to cover all authorized hours with back-up under SVC-08.
A face-to-face review by the PCA supervisor in the client's home of needs, preferences, home safety and the tasks to be done.

procedures: The intake coordinator records the referral date, source, the person referred, contact information, requested services, payer source and requested start date on the intake form.

The intake coordinator makes a first screening for scope. If the person needs nursing or skilled care, medication administration or other services outside nonmedical scope (SVC-01), the agency does not accept the referral for those needs. The intake coordinator tells the referral source and the person, and refers them to appropriate providers. The referral and reason are logged.

For PASSPORT, the intake coordinator confirms with the case management agency that the individual is enrolled in PASSPORT with an open slot and that the services and hours are authorized (OAC 5160-31-03). For the Ohio Home Care Waiver and other Medicaid payers, the coordinator confirms active eligibility and the authorization. The confirmation (who, how, date) is recorded.
The agency does not start services for a Medicaid or PASSPORT client who is not enrolled and authorized. A start date is set only after authorization is confirmed in writing or by system record.

For each authorized or requested schedule, the scheduler and the PCA supervisor perform the staffing check: they list the days and hours required, identify available qualified PCAs for those hours, confirm RN or LPN supervisor capacity to supervise during all scheduled hours (SVC-05), and confirm that the back-up plan can be met (SVC-08).

The Administrator or designee signs the staffing check on the intake form. The check is dated and lists the PCAs and supervisor assigned. A referral is accepted only if the check shows adequate staffing for all of the authorized hours (OAC 173-39-02.11(C)(2)(a)).

If staffing is not adequate, the intake coordinator declines or defers the referral, tells the referral source the same business day, and documents the reason. The agency may re-check if staff become available, and does not promise a start date it cannot meet.

The PCA supervisor schedules the in-home assessment with the client, and visits before or at the first service episode (see SVC-04). Under person-centered planning, the client leads the discussion, may have family or representatives present, and the supervisor uses an interpreter or accessible format as needed (CR-05).

At the assessment, the supervisor reviews the client's needs, preferences and goals; ADL and IADL needs; allergies, dietary needs and advance directives; the home environment for safety and infection-control concerns (SAF-03, SAF-06); who lives in the home; pets; and emergency contacts and medical contacts.

The supervisor identifies any need that falls outside nonmedical scope or any safety risk that cannot be managed. The supervisor discusses this with the client, refers the need to the case manager or physician, and documents it. If the home is unsafe for caregivers and risks cannot be resolved, the Administrator follows SVC-11.
The supervisor reviews with the client the service agreement and rates (CR-06), client rights (CR-01) and the grievance process (CR-02) at or before the assessment.
The supervisor writes the service plan after the assessment (SVC-03) and assigns qualified caregivers who have the competencies the client's needs require (PER-10).
The intake coordinator opens the client record (REC-01) and places in it the referral, authorization proof, staffing check, assessment, signed agreement and service plan.
The Administrator reviews the number of referrals accepted, declined and deferred, and the reasons, every quarter as part of QAPI (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Screens referrals, confirms enrollment and authorization, completes the intake form and documents declines and referrals.
Confirms caregiver availability for the authorized hours and the back-up plan.
Confirms supervisor capacity, performs the in-home assessment before or at the first service episode and identifies out-of-scope needs.
Approves acceptance only when adequate PCA and supervisor staffing is confirmed and reviews intake outcomes.

documentation: Intake form with the signed and dated staffing check
Proof of Medicaid or PASSPORT enrollment, open slot and authorization
In-home assessment
Referral and decline log with reasons
Out-of-scope needs referral record
Client record opening checklist
Quarterly intake review

policies.title: Service Plan and Plan Updates
policies.applies_to: PCA supervisors (RN or LPN), caregivers, intake staff and the Administrator.
policies.purpose: To make sure each client has a written service plan that is person-centered, understood by the client, followed by caregivers, and kept current.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] develops a written service plan for every client with the client leading the planning (OAC 5160-44-02). The plan is in plain language, accessible to people with limited English proficiency and to people with disabilities, signed, and distributed to the client. It includes a back-up plan, allergies, dietary restrictions and advance directives. The plan is reviewed at least every 12 months, when the client's condition significantly changes, or when the client asks. Services follow the plan and the approved hours (OAC 5160-46-04). For clients with a plan from a case management agency, the agency's plan and tasks are consistent with the authorized plan.

definitions.definition: The written plan that lists the services, tasks, schedule, preferences and safety information for the client.
A planning process led by the individual, reflecting the person's preferences, strengths and goals (OAC 5160-44-02).
The steps to be taken so that needed care is still provided if a caregiver or supervisor is unavailable (see SVC-08).
A written document, such as a living will or health care power of attorney, stating a person's health care wishes or naming a decision-maker.
A major change in the client's health, function, living situation or needs that affects the plan or authorized services (see SVC-14).

procedures: After the in-home assessment (SVC-02), the PCA supervisor drafts the service plan with the client, and with any family or representative the client invites. The client states their goals and preferences, such as times, routines, and how tasks are done.

The plan lists: client information and contacts; the tasks to be done by day and visit; authorized hours and schedule; the client's preferences; allergies; dietary restrictions; advance directives and where they are kept; emergency contacts and plans (SAF-05); and the back-up plan.

The back-up plan names who the client or caregiver calls if the caregiver cannot come, how the client will be told, and how the agency will arrange a replacement (SVC-08). The plan includes the agency phone number [PHONE].

The plan is written in plain language at an accessible reading level. For clients with limited English or disabilities, the supervisor provides it in the preferred language or format, with an interpreter if needed (CR-05).
The plan lists only tasks within nonmedical scope (SVC-01). Medication help is described only as reminding, handing the container, opening it, or assisting a physically impaired client (SVC-06).
The client or representative reviews the plan, asks for changes, and signs and dates it. The supervisor signs it too. If the client does not sign, the reason is documented.

The supervisor gives the client a copy on the day of signing, and gives the caregiver the task list before the first visit. Caregivers review the plan with the supervisor. Distribution dates are documented.

Where a case management agency or payer authorizes the plan, the supervisor makes sure the agency plan matches the authorized services and hours, and sends the agency plan to the case manager as required.
Caregivers provide services as in the plan, within the approved hours. They do not add or drop tasks or change hours without supervisor approval (OAC 5160-46-04).

The supervisor reviews the plan with the client at least every 12 months, and sooner at the client's request or when there is a significant change. At each supervisory visit (SVC-04), the supervisor asks whether the plan still meets the client's needs and preferences.

When a caregiver reports a change in condition (SVC-10), the supervisor visits or calls the client within [NUMBER] business days (sooner if urgent), decides whether the plan must change, and starts the update.

If the change is significant, the supervisor notifies the case management agency, ODA or other payer as required in SVC-14, and asks for any change in authorized hours before extra hours are provided.
Each revised plan is signed, copied to the client and caregivers, and filed in the record. Old versions are kept in the record marked as superseded.
The supervisor checks at each plan review that allergies, dietary restrictions, advance directive information and the back-up plan are current.
Plan quality, timeliness of reviews and signatures are audited each quarter under QAPI (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Develops the plan with the client, secures signatures, distributes it, reviews it at least every 12 months and on significant change.
Follow the plan, provide only listed tasks, and report changes or needs for plan changes.
Leads planning, reviews and signs the plan, and asks for changes at any time.
Audits plan completion, timeliness and accessibility.

documentation: Signed service plan with date, including back-up plan, allergies, dietary restrictions and advance directives
Record of plan distribution to client and caregivers
Plan review and update notes
Interpreter or accessible format records
Notices of significant change to case manager or payer
Quarterly plan audit

policies.title: Supervisory Visits
policies.applies_to: PCA supervisors (RN or LPN under RN direction), the Administrator and scheduler.
policies.purpose: To make sure caregivers are supervised in the client's home, that the client's activity plan is set up and kept current, and that every supervisory visit meets the ODA personal care schedule and is documented.
policies.policy: This policy meets OAC 173-39-02.11(C)(4)(b)(i)-(iii), PCA supervisor visits. Only an RN, or an LPN working under RN direction, supervises PCAs (OAC 173-39-02.11(C)(4); see SVC-05). The supervisor makes an initial in-person home visit before or at the first service episode to define the expected activities and develop a written or electronic activity plan. Follow-up visits occur at least every 60 days. A follow-up visit may be done by telephone or video only if at least two in-person visits occur per year. Each visit is documented in the client's record. For Ohio Home Care Waiver clients served by agency aides, OAC 5160-46-04 separately requires an RN or LPN home visit every 60 days, and this agency follows that requirement in addition to this policy (see SVC-13).

definitions.definition: A registered nurse (RN), or a licensed practical nurse (LPN) working under RN direction, who supervises personal care aides.
A written or electronic plan, developed at the initial visit, defining the activities and tasks the caregiver is expected to do for the client.
A face-to-face supervisory visit at the client's home.
A follow-up supervisory contact by telephone or video call, permitted only as described in this policy.

procedures: The scheduler opens a supervisory visit schedule for each new client at intake, showing the initial visit date, the 60-day follow-up due dates and the in-person count for the year.

Before or at the first service episode, the assigned PCA supervisor (RN, or LPN under RN direction) makes an in-person visit to the client's home. If the supervisor cannot be present before the first episode, the first episode is not started until the visit is held, or the supervisor is present at the first episode.

At the initial visit, the supervisor defines with the client the activities the caregiver is expected to do, reviews the home and the client's preferences, and develops the written or electronic activity plan. The plan is consistent with the service plan in SVC-03 and the scope in SVC-01.
The supervisor documents the initial visit in the client's record the same day, listing the date, time, persons present, activities defined, and the activity plan.

Follow-up visits occur at least every 60 days from the date of the previous visit. The scheduler puts the next due date on the schedule at the end of each visit and flags it to the supervisor [NUMBER] days before the 60-day date.

During follow-up visits the supervisor reviews with the client whether services are delivered as planned, the caregiver's performance and conduct, client satisfaction, any change in condition or needs (SVC-10), and whether the activity plan should be changed.

The supervisor may make a follow-up visit by telephone or video only if the client will still receive at least two in-person visits per year. The supervisor tracks the in-person count by 12-month period on the visit schedule and plans in-person visits so that at least two occur in each 12 months of service. If the count would otherwise fall short, the next visit must be in person.

The supervisor does not use telephone or video if the client cannot use it effectively, for example because of hearing, vision or language barriers, or if there are safety or quality concerns. In those cases the visit is in person.
For Ohio Home Care Waiver clients served by agency aides, the RN or LPN makes a home visit every 60 days (OAC 5160-46-04). Telephone or video contact does not replace these home visits.

If a client is hospitalized or services are on hold on the due date, the supervisor documents the reason, and holds the visit within [NUMBER] days after services resume, before or at the first episode back.
A late visit is reported the same day to the Administrator, who records the reason and arranges the visit within [NUMBER] business days. Late visits are logged and reviewed under QAPI (GOV-05).

Each visit is documented in the client's record on the supervisory visit form: date, visit type (in person, telephone or video), time, who participated, observations, client feedback, any plan changes and follow-up needed. The supervisor signs and dates the entry.

The supervisor updates the service plan and activity plan if the visit shows a need, and follows SVC-03 and SVC-14 for significant changes. Caregiver performance concerns are addressed in writing with the caregiver and, when needed, retraining (PER-10).
The Administrator reviews the visit schedule monthly for overdue or missing visits and the in-person count, and reports compliance rates to the governing body each quarter.

responsibilities.role: PCA supervisor (RN or LPN under RN direction)
responsibilities.duty: Makes the initial in-person visit, develops the activity plan, completes follow-up visits at least every 60 days, and documents each visit.
Maintains the visit schedule and reminders and tracks the yearly in-person count.
Reviews visit compliance monthly, approves any late-visit corrective plan and reports to the governing body.
Cooperate with supervisory visits and follow the activity plan and any instructions given.

documentation: Initial visit note and written or electronic activity plan
Supervisory visit forms for every visit (date, type, findings)
Supervisory visit schedule with 60-day due dates and yearly in-person count
Late visit log with reasons and corrective actions
Home Care Waiver 60-day RN or LPN home visit records
Monthly compliance review and quarterly report to the governing body

policies.title: PCA Supervisor Qualifications and Supervision Coverage
policies.applies_to: Administrator, PCA supervisors (RNs and LPNs), schedulers, on-call staff and all personal care aides (PCAs)
policies.purpose: To make sure every PCA is supervised only by a person with the required nursing license, and that a qualified supervisor is assigned and reachable during every hour a PCA is scheduled to work.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] allows only a registered nurse (RN), or a licensed practical nurse (LPN) working under the direction of an RN, to serve as a PCA supervisor. This policy meets OAC 173-39-02.11(C)(4)(a) (PCA supervisor qualifications: only an RN, or an LPN under the direction of an RN, may qualify as a PCA supervisor). An RN or LPN supervises PCAs during all hours PCAs are scheduled to work. This policy meets OAC 173-39-02.11(C)(2)(b) (supervision from an RN or LPN under the direction of an RN during all scheduled hours). The ODH nonmedical home health rules reviewed set no supervisor credential for private-pay clients. [AGENCY NAME] applies the RN/LPN standard to every client, whether PASSPORT, Ohio Home Care Waiver, Older Americans Act or private pay, as one uniform policy. For Older Americans Act personal care, a supervisor is also available during all scheduled hours (OAC 173-3-06.5). The agency does not accept or start a shift for which no qualified supervisor is assigned. Supervisory visit content and timing are in SVC-04.

definitions.definition: An RN, or an LPN working under the direction of an RN, who is assigned to supervise PCAs and who holds a current, unrestricted Ohio license.
The RN named in writing who directs any LPN serving as a PCA supervisor.
Every hour a PCA is scheduled to be in a client's home, including evenings, weekends and holidays.
The RN or LPN designated for a given shift as the person PCAs and clients can reach about care questions or problems.

procedures: Before offering a supervisor position, the Administrator confirms the candidate is an RN or an LPN. No other credential qualifies.

Before the first day of work, the Administrator verifies the license through the Ohio Board of Nursing online license verification. The verification must show an active license with no restrictions that bar the duties. The Administrator prints or saves the result with the date and verifier's initials.
The Administrator places the verification, a copy of the license and the signed job description (PER-03) in the supervisor's personnel file (PER-13).

For each LPN supervisor, the Administrator names a supervising RN in writing. The RN signs a direction statement, and both are kept in the personnel file. The statement describes how the RN directs and reviews the LPN's supervisory work.

The Administrator re-verifies every supervisor's license before its expiration date and at least once every 12 months, and records the result. A lapsed, suspended or restricted license ends that person's supervisory duties immediately. The Administrator reassigns coverage the same day.
The Administrator keeps a supervisor roster showing each supervisor's name, license type and number, expiration date, supervising RN (for LPNs) and last verification date.

The Scheduler builds the weekly schedule so that every PCA shift has a named supervisor assigned for its full length. The Scheduler cannot confirm a shift to a client or PCA unless a supervisor is assigned.

By Thursday of each week, the Scheduler publishes the next week's on-call roster, covering all days, nights, weekends and holidays. The roster lists each supervisor's name and direct on-call phone [PHONE]. The Scheduler gives it to all PCAs and keeps it at the business site.
The Scheduler lists the on-call contact for each shift in the client's visit assignment. Each PCA must know before the shift starts how to reach the supervisor.

If an on-call supervisor cannot cover a shift, they tell the Scheduler as soon as they know. The Scheduler assigns another qualified supervisor and updates the roster before the shift. If no supervisor can be found, SVC-08 applies.

A PCA who cannot reach the on-call supervisor within 15 minutes of an urgent need calls the backup supervisor listed on the roster. The PCA follows SVC-10 in an emergency, and calls 911 first when life or safety is at risk.
Supervisors document each contact with a PCA about care concerns in the client record the same day.

Each quarter, the Administrator compares the schedule, on-call rosters and EVV visit records (SVC-09). The goal is to confirm every PCA hour had a qualified supervisor assigned. Gaps are recorded, corrected and reviewed under GOV-05.
The Administrator accepts no new PASSPORT or other referral unless adequate PCA and supervisor staffing exists for the authorized hours (SVC-02, SVC-12).

responsibilities.duty: Verifies and re-verifies supervisor licenses, names supervising RNs, approves the roster, and audits coverage each quarter.
Keeps a current license, supervises PCAs for assigned shifts, stays reachable on call, and documents contacts.
Directs and reviews the work of any LPN supervisor and signs the direction statement.
Assigns a supervisor to every PCA shift, publishes on-call rosters and escalates gaps to the Administrator.
Knows the on-call contact for each shift and reaches the supervisor for care concerns.

documentation: License verification printout and copy of license in each supervisor's personnel file
LPN supervising-RN direction statement
Supervisor roster with license numbers, expiration and re-verification dates
Weekly on-call roster
Quarterly coverage audit
Supervisor contact notes in the client record

policies.title: Medication Assistance and Self-Administration Support
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, PCAs, supervisors and schedulers
policies.purpose: To limit caregiver involvement with medications to the self-administration help Ohio allows, and to make sure any error is acted on and reported.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] staff do not administer prescribed or over-the-counter (OTC) medications. Staff may only help a client who takes their own medication. Allowed help is to remind the client, hand the client the medication container, open the container, and assist a client who is physically impaired (OAC 3701-60-01 paragraph (Y); OAC 5160-46-04). The client, or the client's legal representative, decides whether and when to take a medication. Staff never make or change that decision. A medication error is a critical incident reportable under OAC 5160-44-05, and it is handled under SAF-02. For Medicaid clients, assistance stays within the person-centered service plan and approved hours (OAC 5160-46-04).

definitions.definition: The client takes their own medication. The client may receive a reminder, have the container handed to them or opened, or receive physical help because of an impairment.
Giving a medication to a client, deciding a dose, or otherwise taking charge of the medication. This is prohibited for agency staff.
Any wrong medication, dose, time or person, a missed dose, or staff conduct beyond permitted assistance. Under OAC 5160-44-05 it is a critical incident.
A client who cannot physically manage a container or take a medication without hands-on help, as documented in the assessment and service plan.

procedures: At intake, the supervisor (RN or LPN) asks who manages the client's medications. The supervisor records the client's ability to self-administer and any physical impairment affecting it (SVC-02).

If a client cannot decide about and direct their own medications, the supervisor tells the client and representative that staff cannot administer them. The supervisor refers them to the case manager or the client's prescriber about other arrangements.
The supervisor writes the permitted medication help into the service plan (SVC-03), using the allowed actions only: remind, hand the container, open the container, and assist the physically impaired.
The supervisor gives each PCA specific, written instructions for that client during orientation to the case. Competency on medication assistance is checked under PER-10.
During a visit, the PCA reminds the client at the time shown in the plan and does not decide when a dose is due.
The PCA hands the container to the client or opens it as the client directs. The client takes the medication.
If the client is physically impaired, the PCA gives only the physical help described in the service plan. The client directs it and the PCA does not choose, adjust or measure a dose.

The PCA does not administer, inject, or pour or measure medication on their own judgment. The PCA does not crush, split or mix medication, or give or suggest any OTC product, herbal product or supplement. The PCA does not change a dose or timing.
If the client refuses, the PCA does not argue or force the medication. The PCA documents the refusal and calls the supervisor the same day.

If the PCA sees a possible error, a wrong or missing medication, a reaction, or something unclear, the PCA calls the on-call supervisor right away. The PCA calls 911 first for any emergency (SVC-10) and stays with the client.

The PCA records each instance of assistance in the task log on the same visit: date, time, type of help, client response and any refusal. The PCA does not record medication names or doses as if giving a dose.

On learning of a possible error, the supervisor takes immediate protective action and follows SAF-02. For waiver clients, the agency reports to the case management agency immediately and no later than 1 business day (OAC 5160-44-05).

The supervisor reviews medication-assistance task-log entries at each supervisory visit (SVC-04) and corrects any practice beyond allowed help. Repeated or serious violations lead to discipline under PER-15.
The agency counts medication errors and refusals in the quarterly quality review (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Assesses ability to self-administer, writes permitted help into the plan, instructs and checks PCAs, and responds to errors.
Gives only the permitted help, logs it, and reports refusals and concerns.
Ensures incident reporting is done and reviews trends.
Decides about and takes the client's own medications.

documentation: Self-administration assessment in the intake record
Medication-assistance section of the service plan
Task log entries for each instance of assistance or refusal
Incident report and critical-incident report for any error
Supervisor review notes
Quarterly quality review data

policies.title: Scheduling, Missed Visits and Continuity of Care
policies.applies_to: Schedulers, PCA supervisors, caregivers and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To make sure authorized services are delivered at the authorized times, that clients get notice of planned changes, and that missed visits are recorded, reported and made up.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] schedules caregivers to deliver each service as authorized or agreed, on the authorized days and at the authorized times. A planned absence is announced with at least 72 hours' notice to the client and, for Medicaid clients, to the case manager (OAC 5160-44-31). A failure to provide an authorized service at the authorized time is a significant change that the agency reports to the case management agency within 1 business day (see SVC-14). For Older Americans Act personal care, staffing must be adequate to cover personal care at least 5 days a week (OAC 173-3-06.5). Changes in the caregiver and in the client's condition or environment are also reported within 24 hours to ODM or its designee for waiver clients (OAC 5160-44-31(B)(17)). Every missed visit is logged with its reason and make-up plan.

definitions.definition: A scheduled or authorized visit that is not delivered, or is delivered substantially late or short of the authorized time, for any reason.
An absence known in advance, such as caregiver leave, a training day or an agency closure.
A visit delivered later to replace a missed one, within the authorization and the client's agreement.
Consistent, uninterrupted delivery of authorized services by qualified caregivers who know the client's plan.

procedures: The Scheduler builds each client's schedule from the service plan or authorization (SVC-03), showing days, start and end times and tasks. Visits are not scheduled beyond approved hours.
The Scheduler assigns a primary caregiver and a named backup to each client where possible, to keep caregivers consistent.
For Older Americans Act clients, the Scheduler checks that staffing covers personal care at least 5 days a week before accepting the referral.
The Scheduler gives each caregiver the week's schedule at least 3 days before it starts and confirms receipt.

A caregiver who cannot make a visit calls the Scheduler or on-call supervisor as soon as they know, and no later than [NUMBER OF HOURS, e.g., 4] hours before the visit unless it is an emergency. Texting alone does not count.
For a planned absence of caregiver or agency, the Scheduler gives the client, and the case manager for Medicaid clients, at least 72 hours' notice with the coverage plan.
On a call-off, the Scheduler immediately tries to fill the visit with a trained backup or float caregiver under SVC-08. The Scheduler tells the client of the change before the visit.
If a visit is late, the caregiver or Scheduler tells the client by phone as soon as the delay is known.
If a visit cannot be covered, the Scheduler tells the client, offers a make-up time, and tells the supervisor and Administrator the same day.
The Scheduler logs every missed visit on the missed-visit log: date, client, authorized time, caregiver, reason, who was told, and make-up plan and date.
The supervisor determines the same day whether the missed visit put the client at risk. If so, the supervisor calls the client or representative and follows SVC-10.

For a waiver or PASSPORT client, the Administrator or supervisor reports the missed authorized service to the case management agency as a significant change within 1 business day (SVC-14). The report is documented in the client record.
If a caregiver change or a client refusal, threat or safety concern is involved for a waiver client, the agency also notifies ODM or its designee within 24 hours (OAC 5160-44-31(B)(17)).
The Scheduler completes the make-up visit within the authorization and with the client's agreement, and records it. A make-up visit is not billed as extra hours beyond those authorized.
A caregiver who is a no-call, no-show or who repeatedly misses visits is counseled under PER-15.
The Administrator reviews the missed-visit log monthly for patterns and reports it in GOV-05.

responsibilities.duty: Builds schedules, gives notices, fills call-offs, and keeps the missed-visit log.
Arrives on time, gives early notice of any absence and reports lateness.
Assesses risk from missed visits and reports significant changes.
Ensures required notices are made and reviews monthly trends.

documentation: Client schedules and caregiver assignments
Notices of planned absence
Missed-visit log with reason and make-up plan
Significant-change report copies
24-hour notification records
Monthly missed-visit review

policies.title: Back-Up Plan for Caregiver or Supervisor Unavailability
policies.applies_to: Administrator, schedulers, PCA supervisors, caregivers and on-call staff
policies.purpose: To make sure personal care continues, or the client is promptly informed and kept safe, when no PCA or no PCA supervisor is available.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains this written back-up plan for providing personal care when no PCA or PCA supervisor is available. This policy meets OAC 173-39-02.11(C)(2)(c) (the provider shall maintain a back-up plan for providing personal care when no PCA or PCA supervisor is available). The plan also meets the back-up plan requirements of OAC 5160-44-31 and OAC 173-3-06.5. Back-up plans are also written into each client's service plan, as required by OAC 5160-44-02. The agency keeps trained back-up caregivers and an on-call rotation of qualified supervisors (SVC-05). The agency tells the client, and the case manager for Medicaid clients, of any gap in coverage.

definitions.definition: The agency's written steps for covering a visit when the scheduled PCA or the supervisor is unavailable. Each client also has an individual back-up plan in the service plan.
A PCA who meets all qualification, background check, orientation and competency requirements and is available to cover visits.
A period when a scheduled visit has no PCA, or a PCA shift has no supervisor.

procedures: The Administrator keeps a pool of back-up PCAs and floats that meet all hiring, background check, orientation and competency requirements (PER-01, PER-04, PER-09, PER-10).
The Administrator maintains an on-call rotation of RN or LPN supervisors, with a second supervisor named as alternate, covering all scheduled PCA hours (SVC-05).

At intake and each plan update, the supervisor works with the client to write an individual back-up plan into the service plan (SVC-03). It lists the back-up caregiver, the contact people, the client's preferences and any informal supports the client chooses. The client signs it.
For waiver and PASSPORT clients, the supervisor sends the back-up plan to the case manager with the service plan.
When a PCA calls off, the Scheduler starts the back-up steps at once. The Scheduler first contacts the client's named back-up caregiver, then the float pool, in order.
The Scheduler aims to have a back-up caregiver confirmed within [30] minutes. The back-up caregiver is briefed on the client's service plan and tasks before the visit.
The Scheduler calls the client to say a different caregiver is coming, who it is, and the arrival time. The Scheduler records the change.

If the PCA supervisor is unavailable, the on-call supervisor takes over. If neither is reachable, the Scheduler calls the alternate supervisor and the Administrator. No PCA works a shift with no supervisor assigned.

If no back-up caregiver can be found, the Scheduler calls the client and representative right away. The Scheduler offers the earliest make-up time and asks whether the client's chosen supports can help in the meantime.
If the client could be at risk without care, the supervisor decides whether to arrange other help, contact the case manager or call emergency services (SVC-10).

For a waiver or PASSPORT client, the Administrator or supervisor notifies the case manager of the gap the same day. The agency reports the failure to deliver an authorized service as a significant change within 1 business day (SVC-14). The agency records the event as a missed visit (SVC-07).
The Scheduler records every back-up activation: date, client, reason, who covered, time of arrival and notices made.

The Administrator reviews the back-up log monthly. If back-up was needed more than [3] times for the same client in a month, the Administrator reviews staffing for that client and the agency's capacity to accept new referrals (SVC-02).
At least once every 12 months, the Administrator tests the plan, including call-tree contacts and phone numbers, and updates rosters. Results go to the GOV-05 review.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the back-up caregiver pool, supervisor on-call rotation and annual plan test.
Runs the back-up call sequence, notifies clients and logs each activation.
Writes individual back-up plans with the client, assesses risk and reports gaps.
Is available as scheduled, is briefed on the client plan and documents the visit.

documentation: This written back-up plan
Back-up caregiver pool list and on-call supervisor roster
Individual back-up plan section in each service plan
Back-up activation log
Client and case manager notification records
Annual plan test record

policies.title: Electronic Visit Verification and Service Verification
policies.applies_to: Caregivers, PCAs, schedulers, billing staff, supervisors and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To keep accurate proof of every visit, to verify Medicaid personal care visits through electronic visit verification (EVV), and to prevent falsified or altered visit records and false billing.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps service verification for every episode of personal care and uses the ODM-approved EVV system for all Medicaid personal care visits. This policy meets OAC 173-39-02.11(C)(6)(a)-(c) (service verification). For each episode the agency retains (i) the service date, (ii) the PCA arrival time, (iii) the PCA departure time, (iv) a description of the activities provided, (v) the name of each PCA in contact with the individual, (vi) the unique identifier of each PCA, and (vii) the unique identifier of the individual. The agency is subject to OAC Chapter 5160-32 (EVV) and ORC 121.36. Personal care aide service billed under HCPCS T1019 is subject to EVV (OAC 5160-58-04), and the EVV record captures service type, recipient, date, location, worker and start and end time. This policy also supports the federal EVV requirement at 42 USC 1396b(l). ODM's EVV system (Sandata) is available to providers at no charge. Falsifying signatures, times or records, and billing for services while a client is hospitalized, are prohibited (OAC 5160-44-31).

definitions.definition: The ODM-approved electronic system that records service type, recipient, date, location, worker and start and end time for a personal care visit.
One visit by a PCA to a client.
The agency- or state-assigned number that identifies a PCA or client in records and EVV.
A correction to an EVV record made after the visit by a person other than the caregiver at the time of service.

procedures: The Administrator completes the required ODM EVV registration and system set-up before the agency provides any Medicaid personal care visit, and confirms the system is in use for every Medicaid visit.
The Administrator assigns each PCA and each client a unique identifier and keeps the key. Identifiers are used on all visit records.
During orientation (PER-09), each PCA is trained on EVV use, including how to check in and out at the client's location. A PCA does not work Medicaid visits until trained.

The PCA checks in at the client's home on arrival and checks out on departure, using the approved method. The PCA never checks in or out for another person, and never records a time that did not occur.
The PCA records on the task log, at the visit, the activities provided in plain terms, matching the service plan.
The task log and EVV together show for each episode: the service date, PCA arrival and departure times, activities, the name and unique ID of each PCA, and the unique client ID.
If the client's signature is not obtained at the visit, the PCA or supervisor obtains it within 3 business days. The reason for the delay is noted.
If a check-in or check-out fails, the PCA tells the Scheduler right away. The Scheduler documents the cause and the actual times the PCA reports.

Only the Scheduler or billing staff member designated by the Administrator makes a manual edit, with the reason, the actual times and the approver recorded. No one edits a time for convenience, to match a schedule or to cover a late or short visit.
Each business day, the Scheduler reviews EVV exceptions (missing check-in or out, location mismatch, short visits). The Scheduler resolves each exception and records the outcome in 5 business days.

Billing staff submit a claim only for a visit with matching EVV and task log records, within authorized hours. Billing staff do not bill for any time the client was hospitalized or not receiving service.
The Administrator reviews a sample of EVV records against task logs and client confirmation every month, and a sample of manual edits every quarter.
A caregiver who falsifies a record, signature or time is removed from client contact at once, investigated and disciplined under PER-15. A confirmed overbilling is corrected and handled under GOV-06.
The agency keeps all service verification records for the retention period in REC-01 and makes them available to regulators and payers on request (REC-03).
For private-pay clients, the agency keeps the same visit records so that the invoice (CR-06) can be checked against actual visit times.

responsibilities.duty: Sets up EVV, assigns identifiers, audits records and edits, and investigates falsification.
Checks in and out accurately and keeps truthful task logs.
Resolves EVV exceptions and makes documented, approved manual edits.
Bills only for verified, authorized visits and never bills during a hospitalization.
Checks task logs at supervisory visits and obtains late client signatures.

documentation: EVV records for each Medicaid visit
Task log with activities and client signature
PCA and client identifier list
EVV exception and manual edit log with reasons and approvals
Monthly and quarterly audit records
Billing reconciliation records

policies.title: Change in Client Condition and Emergencies in the Home
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, PCA supervisors, schedulers and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To make sure caregivers respond safely to emergencies and changes in a client's condition, and that required notices are given on time.
policies.policy: In an emergency, [AGENCY NAME] caregivers call 911 first and then the supervisor. Caregivers do not give medical treatment beyond their scope (SVC-01). For Medicaid waiver clients, the agency notifies ODM or its designee within 24 hours of changes in the client's condition or environment, a change in caregiver, a move, a refusal of services, a threat, or a safety concern (OAC 5160-44-31(B)(17)). The agency takes immediate protective action for any incident and reports it to the case management agency immediately, and no later than 1 business day (OAC 5160-44-05). Incidents are reported under SAF-02. The agency documents each event and notifies the client's family or representative.

definitions.definition: A situation that threatens life, health or safety, such as unresponsiveness, difficulty breathing, chest pain, stroke signs, serious injury, a fall with injury, fire or a violent threat.
A noticeable change in the client's physical, mental or emotional state, abilities, behavior, or home environment that differs from the service plan.
As defined in OAC 5160-44-05, including abuse, neglect, exploitation, medication error, death and a missing person.
The case management agency or other entity ODM names to receive notices for the client.

procedures: At orientation to each client, the caregiver learns the client's address, emergency contacts, known conditions and the on-call supervisor's number [PHONE]. This information is kept in the home or accessible by phone.
In a life-threatening emergency, the caregiver calls 911 first and follows the dispatcher's instructions. The caregiver does not wait for permission.
The caregiver stays with the client, keeps them safe and comfortable, gathers medication and health information to give to responders, and does not move an injured client unless needed for safety.

As soon as the client is safe, the caregiver calls the on-call supervisor. If the supervisor does not answer in 5 minutes, the caregiver calls the alternate supervisor on the roster and then the Administrator.
The supervisor notifies the client's family or representative the same day, and sooner if the client is taken to a hospital. The supervisor records who was told and when.
For a non-emergency change in condition, the caregiver tells the supervisor the same day. The caregiver reports what they saw and when it started, and does not guess a diagnosis.
The supervisor assesses the change by phone or visit within 1 business day, or sooner if risk is high, and decides whether to call the client's physician, case manager or family.
The supervisor updates the service plan if the change is lasting (SVC-03). A significant change triggers plan review and notices under SVC-14.

For a waiver client, the supervisor or Administrator notifies ODM or its designee within 24 hours of a change in condition, environment or caregiver, a move, a refusal, a threat or a safety concern, and records the notice.

If the event is a critical incident or other reportable incident, the supervisor takes immediate protective action and completes SAF-02. The agency reports to the case management agency immediately, and no later than 1 business day (OAC 5160-44-05). Suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation also follows SAF-01.
If the caregiver is hurt or the scene is unsafe, the caregiver leaves the scene, calls 911 and follows SAF-06.
The caregiver writes the event in the task log the same day. The supervisor completes an incident or change-in-condition record within 24 hours.
If the client is hospitalized or goes to a care setting, the supervisor notifies the Scheduler. Visits are held, and no visit is billed while the client is hospitalized (SVC-09).
The Administrator reviews each emergency and change event within 5 business days to check that notices were made and to identify follow-up, retraining or plan changes. Trends go to GOV-05.

responsibilities.duty: Calls 911 in an emergency, then the supervisor; stays with the client and documents the event.
Assesses changes, notifies family and the case manager, updates the plan and completes incident records.
Holds or adjusts visits after hospitalization or move.
Ensures 24-hour and 1-business-day notices are made and reviews each event.

documentation: Task log entry for the event
Incident or change-in-condition report
Record of notices to ODM or designee and case management agency with date and time
Record of family or representative notification
Updated service plan
Administrator review note

policies.title: Discharge, Transfer and Discontinuation of Services
