policies.applies_to: Administrator, supervisors, schedulers, office staff and caregivers; all clients, including private-pay, ODA PASSPORT and Ohio Home Care Waiver clients
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] ends services only for good reason, gives the required written notice, protects client safety during the process, and helps the client move to another provider without a gap in necessary care.
policies.policy: This policy meets OAC 173-39-02(B)(3)(d) (ODA certification item B(3)(d) - Last day of service). [AGENCY NAME] gives the individual and ODA's designee (for PASSPORT clients, the PASSPORT Administrative Agency/case management agency) written notice at least 30 days before the last day of service, except in the circumstances listed in OAC 173-39-02(B)(3)(d). For clients served under an ODM waiver, [AGENCY NAME] gives 30 days' written notice before ending service, or 10 days' written notice when the client has been admitted to a hospital, institution or jail. Where an immediate safety situation makes 30 days' notice unsafe, [AGENCY NAME] acts under the exceptions, protects everyone involved, reports the event, and documents why shorter notice was used. Only the Administrator may approve a discharge or discontinuation. Caregivers never end service on their own or tell a client services are ending. For every discharge, [AGENCY NAME] completes a discharge summary and helps arrange the transition to another provider. For private-pay clients, [AGENCY NAME] applies the same 30-day standard unless the signed service agreement gives the client a longer period.

definitions.definition: Any permanent end of services by [AGENCY NAME], whether the agency, the client or the payer starts it.
The entity ODA names to receive provider notices for a PASSPORT client, normally the PASSPORT Administrative Agency (Council on Aging/Area Agency on Aging) or the case management agency.
The final date on which [AGENCY NAME] will provide an authorized service to the client.
Steps the agency takes so that the client's care continues with another provider, including sharing the service plan with the client's permission and answering the new provider's questions.

procedures: The Administrator reviews every proposed discharge, transfer or discontinuation before any notice goes out. Reasons include client request, loss of funding or authorization, move or admission to a facility, the client's needs exceeding the agency's nonmedical scope, repeated non-payment, an unsafe home environment, or client death.

If the client is the one ending services, the supervisor records the request, the date it was received and the requested last day of service in the client record on the day received. The supervisor confirms the request in writing.

The Administrator decides whether the 30-day notice applies or whether an exception in OAC 173-39-02(B)(3)(d) applies. The Administrator reads the current rule text and records the decision and the reasoning in the client record.

For standard discharges, the Administrator or designee prepares a written notice on [DISCHARGE NOTICE FORM]. The notice states the reason, the last day of service (at least 30 days after the notice date), the client's right to file a grievance (see CR-02), and how to ask for help finding another provider.
The notice is delivered to the client or authorized representative by hand with a signed acknowledgment or by mail with proof of mailing. A copy goes into the client record.

The notice is sent on the same day to ODA's designee for PASSPORT clients, and to the case management agency or ODM designee for Ohio Home Care Waiver or other Medicaid waiver clients. Proof of transmission (email confirmation, fax report or mail receipt) is kept in the client record.

When a waiver client is in a hospital, institution or jail, the agency gives written notice at least 10 days before the last day of service. The Administrator documents the admission date and the source of the information.

If a client's own behavior or the home creates an immediate threat to a caregiver or the client, the supervisor removes the caregiver at once, calls 911 if needed, and tells the Administrator right away. The Administrator decides the same day whether the exception applies and documents the facts, the people notified and the date and time.

The Administrator reports an immediate-safety discontinuation to the payer's designee within 1 business day, and the event is reported under SVC-14 and SAF-02. Any suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation is reported under SAF-01.
Between the notice date and the last day of service, the agency keeps providing all authorized services unless safety requires otherwise. The scheduler continues to staff visits according to SVC-07.

Within the first 7 days after notice, the supervisor offers the client or representative a list of other providers, or refers the client to the case management agency or Council on Aging, and records what was offered.

With the client's written permission, the supervisor shares the current service plan, medication assistance needs, allergies, dietary restrictions and advance directive information with the receiving provider, and documents what was sent and when.

The supervisor completes a discharge summary within 7 days after the last day of service. It includes the dates of service, reason for discharge, the client's condition and status at discharge, notices given, and transition arrangements.

The office returns the client's property and documents, stops scheduling, closes the client's EVV and billing schedule in coordination with SVC-09 and SVC-12, and sends a final invoice or confirms that billing is complete.

If a client dies, the Administrator notifies the payer's designee as required, reports it under SAF-02 when it qualifies as a critical incident, and completes the discharge summary using the date of death as the last day of service.
The record is closed and retained according to REC-01. The Administrator reviews all discharges quarterly as part of GOV-05 to identify patterns.

responsibilities.duty: Approves all discharges, determines whether an exception applies, signs notices, and makes sure payer notices are sent on time.
Delivers notices, offers transition help, keeps services in place until the last day of service, and writes the discharge summary.
Maintain visits through the last day, send notices to the designee, and file proof of transmission.
Continues care as scheduled, tells the supervisor of any client statement about stopping services, and does not discuss discharge decisions with the client.

documentation: Discharge request or decision memo with reason and exception determination
Signed written notice to client and proof of delivery
Proof of notice transmission to ODA's designee or ODM designee/case management agency
List of alternate providers offered
Transition record, including client permission to share information
Discharge summary
Safety-exception documentation, if used
Quarterly discharge review in QA files

policies.title: Coordination with Medicaid Programs and Payers
policies.applies_to: Administrator, billing staff, supervisors and office staff; all Medicaid-funded clients
policies.purpose: To define how [AGENCY NAME] works with the ODA PASSPORT program, the Ohio Home Care Waiver and other payers so that services are authorized, delivered as planned, billed correctly and reported on time.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is licensed by ODH as a nonmedical home health services provider. Medicaid funding is a separate step with separate requirements. The agency pursues two pathways: (1) ODA PASSPORT personal care, under OAC Chapter 173-39 (personal care is defined in OAC 173-39-02.11), and (2) the ODM Ohio Home Care Waiver, under OAC Chapter 5160-46 (billing rules are in OAC 5160-46-06). The agency does not bill any Medicaid program until it holds the needed certification or enrollment, and the Administrator has confirmed the current enrollment status, rates and referral rules with ODM and the local Council on Aging/Area Agency on Aging. The agency accepts PASSPORT referrals only for individuals who are enrolled and authorized, as OAC 5160-31-03 requires. The agency acknowledges OAC 5160-44-05 in writing at ODM enrollment and every year after that, as required by OAC 5160-44-31. It completes new-provider training within 90 days of ODM enrollment, and it reports contact changes to ODM or its designee within 7 days. Services delivered to waiver or PASSPORT clients follow the person-centered service plan consistent with 42 CFR 441.301(c), and no more than the authorized units are provided.

definitions.definition: Ohio Department of Aging's Medicaid waiver program, which provides home and community-based services to eligible older adults through certified providers.
ODM's Medicaid waiver for individuals who need home care, including personal care aide services under OAC Chapter 5160-46.
The agency that develops the individual's plan and authorizes services (for PASSPORT, the PASSPORT Administrative Agency).
Written approval from the payer or case management agency stating the service, units and dates the agency may provide and bill.
The plan developed with the individual that sets out the authorized services and goals; see SVC-03.

procedures: Before applying to any Medicaid program, the Administrator confirms with ODM the current status of Medicaid provider enrollment, including any enrollment pause or moratorium that may apply to personal care aide or related provider types, and records the answer and date in the compliance file.

The Administrator confirms with ODA and the local Council on Aging/Area Agency on Aging the steps to become a PASSPORT provider, including the recommendation process, and keeps a checklist of each step and its completion date.
The Administrator confirms the Medicaid provider application fee and whether any waiver of the fee applies, and obtains approval from the governing body before payment.
The Administrator confirms which Ohio Home Care Waiver provider requirements apply and follows SVC-13 before enrolling for that waiver.

When the agency receives a referral, office staff check that the individual is enrolled in the program and that there is a written authorization naming the service, units and dates. Referrals without authorization are not scheduled and are returned to the referring agency.

The supervisor obtains the person-centered service plan or plan of care from the case management agency and builds the agency's service plan from it under SVC-03. Services outside the authorized plan are not provided.
The scheduler staffs visits only within authorized units and times. Hours above the authorization require written approval from the case management agency before the visit.

Within 1 business day of any event that triggers notice, the supervisor follows SVC-14 to notify ODA's designee or the case management agency. Ohio Home Care Waiver clients may also require additional ODM notices, which the Administrator confirms and sends on time.

At ODM enrollment, the Administrator and each person responsible for services sign a written acknowledgment of OAC 5160-44-05. The Administrator repeats this every year within 12 months of the last acknowledgment and files it in the compliance file.
The Administrator completes the ODM new-provider training within 90 days of enrollment and keeps the completion record. Billing staff and supervisors review the training content as well.

Any change in agency name, address, email or phone is reported to ODM or its designee within 7 days, and to ODA and the Council on Aging as their rules require. The Administrator records the date and the method of each report.
Services are verified electronically under SVC-09. Billing staff only bill units that have a matching verified visit, a signed task log and a current authorization.

Billing staff read the current text of the applicable billing rules before the first claim and each time the Administrator is told of a rule change, and they use the rate and unit schedule currently published by the payer. The rate used is documented on each claim batch.
Billing staff reconcile claims against EVV and authorizations monthly. Overbilling, underbilling, or unauthorized service is reported to the Administrator at once and handled under GOV-06.
The Administrator reviews payer correspondence, audit requests and remittance problems within 5 business days and keeps a log of responses.
The Administrator reviews this policy and the payer requirements at least annually under GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Confirms enrollment status, rates and referral rules with ODM, ODA and the Council on Aging, signs required acknowledgments, completes training and ensures timely reports.
Check authorizations and EVV before billing, reconcile claims monthly and use current rates and rules.
Aligns the agency service plan with the payer's plan and reports significant changes.
Accept only authorized referrals and schedule within authorized units.

documentation: ODM enrollment status confirmation and fee records
PASSPORT provider steps checklist
Referral and authorization files
Annual OAC 5160-44-05 acknowledgments
New-provider training completion record
Contact-change notices and proof of transmission
Billing reconciliation records and payer correspondence log

policies.title: Ohio Home Care Waiver Personal Care Aide Requirements
policies.applies_to: Administrator, supervisors, RN/LPN supervisory staff, caregivers and billing staff; applies only if [AGENCY NAME] enrolls with ODM to provide Ohio Home Care Waiver services
policies.purpose: To set out the additional requirements that apply when [AGENCY NAME] provides personal care aide services under the Ohio Home Care Waiver, and to prevent the agency from providing or billing services it is not qualified to offer.
policies.policy: This policy applies only if [AGENCY NAME] enrolls with ODM for the Ohio Home Care Waiver. Many of these requirements go beyond ODH nonmedical licensure. Before the agency accepts any Ohio Home Care Waiver client, the Administrator confirms that every requirement below is met. Under OAC 5160-46-04(E), an agency personal care aide must be employed by a Medicare-certified or otherwise accredited agency. If [AGENCY NAME] does not hold that status, it does not provide agency-based aide services under this waiver and does not bill them. Services follow the person-centered service plan (PCSP) and are limited to approved hours (OAC 5160-46-04(A)-(D)). Agency aides must have an ODH or Medicare competency certificate, first aid training, and 8 hours of in-service training each year. A non-agency aide completes 6 hours. An RN or LPN visits the client's home at least every 60 days. Aides do not administer prescribed or over-the-counter medications. They may help only with self-administration, as set out in SVC-06. The home care attendant service (S5125, OAC 5160-46-06.1) includes nursing tasks that are outside the nonmedical scope, and [AGENCY NAME] does not provide it unless it is separately enrolled and has qualified nursing oversight. Billing follows OAC 5160-46-06. A confidential clinical record is kept at the place of business as required by OAC 5160-46-04(I)-(J).

definitions.definition: The person-centered service plan that authorizes the personal care aide services and approved hours.
Documentation from ODH or a Medicare-recognized program showing the aide has passed a competency evaluation; see PER-10.
Annual training hours the aide must complete (8 hours for agency aides, 6 hours for non-agency aides); see PER-11.
A visit to the client's home by an RN or LPN at least every 60 days to review the aide's work and the client's status; see SVC-04.
A waiver service that includes nursing tasks; not provided by [AGENCY NAME] unless separately enrolled and staffed.

procedures: Before enrolling, the Administrator reviews OAC 5160-46-04 and 5160-46-06 and confirms in writing whether [AGENCY NAME] is Medicare-certified or accredited as required for agency aides. The Administrator records the finding and date in the compliance file. If the requirement is not met, no agency aide services are provided or billed under this waiver.
The Administrator confirms with ODM that enrollment for the relevant provider type is open, following SVC-12.
The governing body approves the decision to enroll and confirms that an RN or LPN is available for supervisory visits.

Before any aide is assigned, PER-02 staff verify and file the aide's ODH or Medicare competency certificate, first aid certification and background check results. Aides without all three are not assigned.

The supervisor obtains the PCSP and approved hours from the case management agency and enters them in the scheduling and EVV system. The scheduler never schedules above the approved hours without written authorization.
Aides follow the task list in the PCSP. Tasks not in the PCSP are not performed, and the aide tells the supervisor if the client asks for them.

Aides do not administer medications, including over-the-counter products. They may remind the client, hand the container, open it, or physically assist a client who has a physical impairment, as described in SVC-06. They document each instance and report any error immediately.

An RN or LPN makes a home visit at least every 60 days for each client. The scheduler sets the next due date when each visit is completed. The nurse documents the visit using the SVC-04 supervisory visit form.
If a 60-day visit is at risk of being late, the nurse notifies the Administrator at least 10 days before the due date and the visit is scheduled within the 60-day period.

The training coordinator tracks each aide's annual in-service hours (8 hours for agency aides; 6 hours for non-agency aides) and notifies the aide and supervisor 60 days before the annual deadline. Aides who are behind are not scheduled until the hours are complete.

Records staff keep a confidential clinical record at the business site for each client. It contains identification data, the PCSP, allergies and dietary restrictions, advance directives, the task log with times and dated signatures, signed progress notes, and a discharge summary. See REC-01.
Billing staff bill only units supported by a verified EVV visit, a signed task log and the current authorization, using OAC 5160-46-06 and the current ODM fee schedule.

If a client or case manager asks for home care attendant service (S5125) or any nursing task, the supervisor declines, explains that it is outside the agency's scope, and refers the request to the case management agency. The Administrator notes the referral in the record.
The Administrator audits compliance with this policy quarterly, covering certificates, in-service hours, supervisory visits and billing, and reports the results to the governing body under GOV-05.

responsibilities.duty: Confirms eligibility to enroll, approves assignments, audits compliance and keeps the compliance file.
Visits each client at least every 60 days, documents the visit and reports problems.
Tracks competency certificates, first aid and in-service hours.
Bill only verified, authorized units under the current rules.
Performs only PCSP tasks, helps only with self-administration of medication and keeps a signed task log.

documentation: Written determination of Medicare certification/accreditation status
Governing body approval of enrollment
Aide competency certificates and first aid records
In-service hour tracking log
60-day RN/LPN visit records and tracking calendar
PCSP and authorization records

policies.title: Significant Change Notices to ODA or Case Management Agency
policies.applies_to: Administrator, supervisors, schedulers, office staff and caregivers; all ODA PASSPORT clients and other clients whose services are managed by a case management agency
policies.purpose: To make sure that significant changes affecting a client's service needs or safety are reported to ODA or its designee within one business day.
policies.policy: This policy meets OAC 173-39-02(B)(3)(b) (ODA certification item B(3)(b) - Significant changes). [AGENCY NAME] notifies ODA or its designee no later than one business day after becoming aware of a significant change affecting the individual's service needs or safety. The listed changes are: (i) not providing an authorized service at the authorized time; (ii) the individual moving; (iii) repeated refusal of services; (iv) any incident subject to OAC 5160-44-05; and (v) any other significant change in the individual's status or environment. Caregivers report any of these to the supervisor immediately, and the supervisor or Administrator sends the notice using the agency notice form. Proof of transmission is kept. Where an event is also an incident under OAC 5160-44-05, the agency takes immediate protective action and reports it to the case management agency immediately and no later than one business day (see SAF-02). A significant-change notice is not a substitute for a report to Adult Protective Services (see SAF-01) or for emergency calls to 911.

definitions.definition: Any of the five listed changes in OAC 173-39-02(B)(3)(b)(i)-(v) that affects the individual's service needs or safety.
The moment any agency employee, including a caregiver, learns of the change. The one-business-day clock starts at that moment, not when a supervisor learns of it.
A day other than a Saturday, Sunday or state or federal holiday on which state offices are open.
The entity ODA directs the provider to notify, normally the PASSPORT Administrative Agency or case management agency.

procedures: Caregivers report any of the five triggers to the supervisor by phone as soon as they know, and no later than the end of the shift. Examples are a missed visit, a client who has moved or is moving, a client who refuses care, an injury or fall, or a change in the home.
If the supervisor cannot be reached, the caregiver calls the on-call line at [PHONE] so that the report is not delayed. For emergencies the caregiver calls 911 first (see SVC-10).
The supervisor opens a significant-change log entry noting the date and time the agency became aware, the client, the trigger category (i-v), and who reported it.

Trigger (i), service not provided at the authorized time: the scheduler tells the supervisor the same day a visit is missed, late or cut short. The supervisor applies SVC-07 and SVC-08 to arrange coverage and sends the notice within one business day of the missed time.

Trigger (ii), the individual moves: when the client, family or staff learn of a move, an admission to a facility or a planned move, the supervisor sends the notice within one business day, including the new address if known.

Trigger (iii), repeated refusal of services: the supervisor documents each refusal with date and reason. When a refusal occurs a second time within the same authorization period or the pattern shows repeated refusal, the supervisor sends the notice within one business day of becoming aware of the pattern.

Trigger (iv), incidents under OAC 5160-44-05: the Administrator or supervisor takes immediate protective action and reports to the case management agency immediately and no later than one business day, following SAF-02.

Trigger (v), other significant change: the supervisor decides, with the Administrator when unsure, whether a change in the client's health, mental status, function, caregiver support, finances or home environment affects service needs or safety. If in doubt, the agency sends the notice.

The supervisor completes the notice on [SIGNIFICANT CHANGE NOTICE FORM] stating the client's name, program, date and time of the event, what happened, the date and time the agency became aware, actions taken, and who to contact.
The notice is sent to ODA's designee or the case management agency by the method that agency has told [AGENCY NAME] to use, no later than one business day after the agency became aware.
The sender keeps proof of transmission (email confirmation, fax report, portal receipt or call log with the name of the person reached) and files it with the notice in the client record.
The supervisor follows up within 2 business days to confirm the notice was received, and records any instructions given by the case manager.
If the notice is late for any reason, the Administrator sends it right away, writes a brief explanation, and reviews the cause for corrective action under GOV-05.
If the event also concerns suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, the supervisor makes the APS report under SAF-01 without waiting to send the significant-change notice.
The Administrator reviews the significant-change log monthly and reports trends to the quality assurance committee.

responsibilities.duty: Reports any trigger to the supervisor or on-call line promptly and writes it in the visit notes.
Logs the change, completes and sends the notice within one business day, and files proof of transmission.
Reports missed or late authorized services the same day.
Makes close calls on whether a change is significant, ensures notices are on time, and reviews the log.

documentation: Significant-change log
Completed notice form
Proof of transmission
Visit notes and refusal documentation
Case manager follow-up notes
Late-notice explanation and corrective action, if any
Monthly log review notes

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors and volunteers; all clients
policies.purpose: To protect clients from abuse, neglect and exploitation, to require immediate reporting of any reasonable cause to believe it has occurred, and to set out the agency's prevention measures.
policies.policy: This policy meets OAC 173-39-02(B)(3)(a) (ODA certification item B(3)(a) - APS reporting). [AGENCY NAME] has zero tolerance for abuse, neglect and exploitation of clients. Any employee, contractor or volunteer who has reasonable cause to believe that a client has suffered abuse, neglect or exploitation reports it to the local county Adult Protective Services (APS) program under ORC 5101.63, and tells a supervisor or the Administrator. The Administrator also notifies ODA or its designee within one business day. [AGENCY NAME] takes immediate protective action and reports any incident to the case management agency immediately and no later than one business day, as OAC 5160-44-05 requires. Staff may not abuse or neglect clients, and any employee who does will be removed from client contact and terminated and reported to the appropriate authorities. The Administrator confirms the current reporter list, timing and report content of ORC 5101.63 with the county APS program at hire of the Administrator and annually. Reports are made in good faith. [AGENCY NAME] does not retaliate against anyone who reports, and staff do not have to prove abuse before reporting. Staff do not investigate and do not confront the suspected abuser.

definitions.definition: Knowingly causing physical harm, serious emotional or psychological harm, or sexual abuse, or placing the client in a situation that causes this, including by a caregiver, family member or other person. The agency uses the definitions in the current ORC 5101.60.
Failure of a caregiver to provide the goods or services needed to avoid physical harm, mental anguish or mental illness, or the client's self-neglect.
Unlawful or improper use of a client's resources, including money, property or benefits, for another person's benefit; see CR-04.
A good-faith belief based on what the staff member saw, heard or was told. Certainty is not required.
The county Adult Protective Services program in the county where the client lives.

procedures: At orientation and each year, all staff receive training on recognizing and reporting abuse, neglect and exploitation, and sign an acknowledgment that they have read this policy (see PER-09 and PER-11).

The office posts the county APS number, [COUNTY APS PHONE], for each county served, and the agency hotline for staff reports, [PHONE], in the office and in each caregiver's packet. The Administrator checks the numbers every year and updates them.
If a client is in immediate danger or needs emergency care, the staff member calls 911 first and stays with the client if it is safe to do so.

Any staff member who has reasonable cause to believe abuse, neglect or exploitation has occurred reports it right away to county APS by phone. They do not wait for a supervisor's approval and do not wait until the end of the shift. The agency's standard is to report during the same shift or the same day.

The staff member also tells the supervisor or Administrator immediately. If the suspected abuser is the supervisor or Administrator, the staff member reports directly to APS and to the governing body at [PHONE].

The supervisor takes immediate protective action: separating the client from the suspected person where lawful and safe, arranging medical care, removing any involved caregiver from the client's schedule and securing evidence such as records and logs.

The Administrator notifies ODA or its designee within one business day of becoming aware, and reports the incident to the case management agency immediately and no later than one business day, using the report contents required by OAC 5160-44-05. This is done together with SAF-02.
The person who made the report completes the incident report under SAF-02 within 24 hours, stating facts only: who, what, when, where, what was seen or said, and what actions were taken.

The Administrator enters the APS report in the APS log with the date and time, the APS contact and any case number, the person who reported, and the notices sent to ODA's designee or the case management agency.
The Administrator cooperates fully with APS, ODA, ODM, law enforcement and the case management agency, and does not interfere with any interview or investigation.

When the suspected person is an employee, the Administrator immediately removes the person from all client contact pending the investigation. The Administrator reviews whether the person's conduct requires action under PER-08 and PER-15 and whether other reports to licensing bodies are needed.
Agency staff do not investigate the allegation themselves and do not ask the client leading questions. They listen, offer comfort and document the client's own words.
The Administrator informs the client or representative of the report unless doing so would put the client at risk, and offers help in contacting the case manager.
No one is punished or retaliated against for a good-faith report. Retaliation is grounds for discipline up to termination.

To prevent abuse, the agency completes background checks under PER-04 through PER-08, supervises caregivers under SVC-04, bans caregivers from handling client funds and accepting gifts under CR-04, and reviews complaints under CR-02.
The Administrator reviews the APS log quarterly with the QA process in GOV-05 and takes corrective action on any pattern.

responsibilities.duty: Report reasonable cause to APS immediately and tell a supervisor; never retaliate or investigate.
Takes immediate protective action, secures records and supports the reporter.
Notifies ODA or its designee and the case management agency within one business day, maintains the APS log and posts the APS numbers.
Receives reports involving the Administrator and reviews the quarterly summary.

documentation: APS log
Incident report
Notices to ODA or its designee and the case management agency, with proof of transmission
Annual training records and signed policy acknowledgments
Posted APS numbers verification
Personnel actions related to the allegation
Quarterly APS log review

policies.title: Incident Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors and volunteers; Administrator and supervisors; all clients
policies.purpose: To make sure that every incident involving a client, caregiver or the agency is documented, reviewed, reported to the proper authorities on time and used to improve safety.
policies.policy: This policy meets OAC 173-39-02(A)(7) (ODA certification item A(7) - Incident reporting), which requires a written or electronic policy on documenting incidents that complies with paragraph (B)(3)(b) of the rule. [AGENCY NAME] documents every incident in writing. Staff complete the incident report within 24 hours of the incident (agency policy). Critical incidents under OAC 5160-44-05 include abuse, neglect, exploitation, medication error, death and a missing person. For any incident, the agency takes immediate protective action and reports it to the case management agency immediately and no later than one business day, using the report contents that OAC 5160-44-05 requires. Incidents that are significant changes under OAC 173-39-02(B)(3)(b) are also reported to ODA or its designee within one business day (see SVC-14). Suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation is also reported to APS (see SAF-01). The Administrator reviews each incident, decides what follow-up is needed and tracks trends through quality assurance.

definitions.definition: Any unusual event that affects or could affect a client's health or safety, a caregiver's safety, client property or the agency, including falls, injuries, medication errors, property damage, allegations of abuse, theft, emergencies and threats.
An incident defined in OAC 5160-44-05, including abuse, neglect, exploitation, medication error, death and a missing person.
Steps taken at once to make the client safe, such as calling 911, getting medical care, separating the client from a source of harm or removing a caregiver from the schedule.
The agency that authorizes and coordinates the client's services; the recipient of the one-business-day incident report.

procedures: A staff member who witnesses or learns of an incident takes immediate protective action first: calls 911 for emergencies, gives first aid within training, and stays with the client if safe.
The staff member notifies the supervisor or the on-call line at [PHONE] immediately and no later than the end of the shift. Critical incidents are reported by phone right away.

The staff member completes [INCIDENT REPORT FORM] within 24 hours of the incident. The report states facts only: who, what, when, where, witnesses, injuries, what the client said, actions taken and who was notified.
The supervisor reviews the report within 1 business day, makes sure the client is safe and writes follow-up actions on the form.

The supervisor classifies the incident: critical incident under OAC 5160-44-05, other incident, or not a reportable incident. When unsure, the supervisor asks the Administrator, and the incident is treated as critical until decided otherwise.

For a critical incident, the Administrator or designee reports to the case management agency immediately and no later than one business day, using the contents OAC 5160-44-05 requires. The Administrator keeps the current report form and checks it annually.

For a medication error, the supervisor documents what was given or not given, the time, the client's condition, the prescriber or pharmacist contacted if any, and the steps to prevent it from happening again. The error is reported as a critical incident. See SVC-06.

For a death, the Administrator reports it to the case management agency and, if it meets a trigger, ODA's designee within one business day, and documents the circumstances. If the death is unexpected, the staff member also calls 911.

For a missing client, the caregiver searches the home and immediate area, calls 911 if the client is not found quickly, and notifies the supervisor. The agency reports it immediately as a critical incident.
For suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, follow SAF-01 to make the APS report and the one-business-day notices.

If the incident is also a significant change under OAC 173-39-02(B)(3)(b), the supervisor sends the notice within one business day under SVC-14. One report may serve for both if it meets both requirements.
For theft, property damage or loss, the Administrator follows the loss claim instructions in GOV-08 and notifies the client of how to file a claim.
For caregiver injuries or exposures, follow SAF-04 and SAF-06 and file any required workers' compensation reports.

The Administrator enters each incident in the incident log, with the dates the incident occurred and the report was made, the agencies notified, proof of transmission and the follow-up completed. Proof of transmission is kept with the report.

The Administrator reviews the incident log monthly and reports to the quality assurance committee quarterly under GOV-05, looking at trends by client, caregiver, time and type, and documenting corrective actions.

Incident reports are kept in the client record and in a confidential incident file, and are retained as set out in REC-01. They are available to ODA, ODM, ODH and other authorized reviewers (see REC-03). No staff member is penalized for making a good-faith report.

responsibilities.duty: Protects the client, notifies the supervisor and completes the incident report within 24 hours.
Reviews the report, classifies it and ensures follow-up.
Makes required external reports on time, keeps the incident log and leads trend review.
Reviews incident data quarterly and recommends corrective actions.

documentation: Completed incident report
Incident log
Proof of transmission of reports to the case management agency, ODA's designee and APS where applicable
Follow-up and corrective action notes
Quarterly QA incident trend review
Current OAC 5160-44-05 report form

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, PCA supervisors, office staff who enter client homes, and volunteers; all programs (private pay, ODA PASSPORT personal care, ODM Ohio Home Care Waiver)
policies.purpose: To reduce the risk of infection for clients and staff by requiring standard precautions, adequate protective supplies, trained staff, and exclusion of ill staff from client contact.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] applies standard precautions in every client home. Before any in-person client contact, every caregiver completes orientation that includes standard precautions for infection control, as required by OAC 173-39-02.11(C)(3)(b) (citation C26). The agency provides gloves and other personal protective equipment (PPE) at no cost to staff and trains staff on handwashing, linen handling and waste handling. Staff with a communicable illness do not work with clients. The agency follows current guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the Ohio Department of Health (ODH). Where staff may be exposed to blood or other potentially infectious materials, the agency also follows SAF-04 and 29 CFR 1910.1030. This policy is part of the agency's infection control program and does not authorize caregivers to perform skilled nursing tasks (see SVC-01).

definitions.definition: Infection control practices applied to all clients regardless of diagnosis: hand hygiene, PPE, respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette, safe handling of sharps, linen and waste, and cleaning of surfaces and equipment.
Personal protective equipment such as disposable gloves, masks, gowns and eye protection.
An illness that can spread from person to person, such as influenza, COVID-19, infectious gastroenteritis, scabies, or infectious skin or eye conditions.
Body fluids and materials defined in 29 CFR 1910.1030 that may carry bloodborne pathogens.

procedures: Before any in-person client contact, the PCA supervisor or designated trainer delivers the standard precautions module during orientation (PER-09) and records the date, trainer and caregiver signature on the orientation checklist.

The Administrator, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], maintains a written infection control reference for caregivers based on current CDC and ODH guidance and reviews it at least annually and whenever CDC or ODH issues new guidance that affects home care.

Orientation and annual in-service training (PER-11) cover hand hygiene (when and how to wash, when to use alcohol-based rub), glove use and removal, respiratory etiquette, and when to use a mask or other PPE.
Training also covers handling of soiled linen (wear gloves, do not shake, bag soiled linen at the point of use, launder per client's washing instructions using the hottest appropriate water setting).
Training also covers waste handling: double-bag heavily soiled disposables, place in the client's household trash, and never place needles or sharps in household trash (see SAF-04).

The agency supplies each caregiver with a PPE kit (gloves, masks, hand sanitizer, disposable bags) at orientation. Caregivers request resupply from the office by phone at [PHONE]; the office replaces supplies within one business day.

Caregivers wash or sanitize hands on arrival, before and after meal preparation, before and after personal care, after toileting assistance, after handling soiled linen or waste, after removing gloves, and before leaving the home.
Caregivers wear gloves for any contact with blood, body fluids, broken skin, mucous membranes, or soiled items, and change gloves between tasks and between clients.
Caregivers clean and disinfect client-use surfaces and shared equipment when the service plan includes home management, using products the client has in the home or those the agency provides.

A caregiver who has fever, vomiting, diarrhea, an undiagnosed rash, a suspected or confirmed communicable illness, or who has been told to isolate must not report to a client's home and must call the office at [PHONE] before the shift begins.
The scheduler records the absence, activates the back-up plan under SVC-08 so the client is not left without authorized care, and informs the PCA supervisor.

The PCA supervisor decides on return to work using current CDC and ODH guidance and, when needed, written clearance from the caregiver's health care provider. The decision is documented in the personnel record.

If a client has a suspected or known communicable illness, the caregiver notifies the PCA supervisor, follows the PPE instructions the supervisor gives, and the supervisor informs the client's case manager or physician as appropriate and documents the communication (SVC-10).
Exposure to blood or body fluids is handled under SAF-04 and reported under SAF-02. Employee health and TB screening requirements are handled under PER-12.
The Administrator reviews infection-related incidents, absences and complaints at least quarterly through the quality assurance program (GOV-05) and updates training and supplies as needed.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains this program, ensures PPE supply, ensures guidance is current, and reviews infection-related events quarterly.
Delivers or oversees training, decides on staff return to work, and advises caregivers on client-specific precautions.
Replaces ill staff through the back-up plan and logs absences.
Applies standard precautions, uses PPE, and reports illness before the shift.

documentation: Orientation checklist showing standard precautions training completed before client contact
Annual in-service attendance records
PPE issue and resupply log
Illness absence and return-to-work records in the personnel file
Infection-related incident reports and quarterly QA review minutes

policies.title: Bloodborne Pathogens Exposure Control
policies.applies_to: All employees with occupational exposure to blood or other potentially infectious materials; all programs
policies.purpose: To protect employees from occupational exposure to bloodborne pathogens such as hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus and HIV, as required by the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard (29 CFR 1910.1030).
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] complies with 29 CFR 1910.1030 wherever employees have occupational exposure to blood or other potentially infectious materials (OPIM). The agency conducts and documents an exposure determination. If exposure is reasonably anticipated for any job classification, the agency maintains a written exposure control plan, provides training, PPE and sharps handling instructions, offers hepatitis B vaccine, and provides post-exposure evaluation and follow-up at no cost to the employee. Caregivers do not perform tasks involving sharps, injections, blood glucose testing, or wound care beyond the scope in SVC-01, but they may still be exposed through client bleeding, soiled linen, or discarded sharps found in the home. The Administrator verifies this policy against the current text of 29 CFR 1910.1030 at each annual review.

definitions.definition: Reasonably anticipated skin, eye, mucous membrane, or parenteral contact with blood or OPIM that may result from the performance of an employee's duties.
A specific eye, mouth, other mucous membrane, non-intact skin, or parenteral contact with blood or OPIM that results from the performance of an employee's duties.
The agency's written plan that identifies job classifications and tasks with exposure, and describes methods of compliance, vaccination, training, and post-exposure follow-up.
Treating all human blood and certain body fluids as if known to be infectious for bloodborne pathogens.
Needles, lancets, broken glass and any object that can penetrate skin.

procedures: The Administrator, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], and the PCA supervisor perform a written exposure determination listing every job classification (caregiver, PCA supervisor, office staff) and tasks in which occupational exposure may occur, without regard to PPE. This is completed before the agency begins services and reviewed annually.

If exposure is anticipated for any classification, the Administrator prepares a written exposure control plan that includes the exposure determination, methods of compliance, hepatitis B vaccination, post-exposure evaluation, training, and recordkeeping. The plan is reviewed and updated at least annually and when tasks change, and is available to employees on request.
The agency provides, at no cost, gloves, masks, eye protection, gowns, and other PPE appropriate to the task, and replaces PPE that is torn or contaminated.

Within 10 working days of initial assignment to a job with exposure, and at no cost, the agency offers hepatitis B vaccination to each exposed employee, unless the employee has already been vaccinated, is immune, or medically cannot take it. Declination is documented on a signed declination form, and the employee may accept later at no cost.

Before assignment to tasks with exposure, and annually thereafter, employees receive training that covers the standard, the epidemiology and symptoms of bloodborne diseases, modes of transmission, the exposure control plan, PPE use, vaccine information, emergency procedures, and post-exposure steps. A person knowledgeable about the topic is available to answer questions.

Caregivers treat all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious, wear gloves for any contact, and clean up spills with the client's household disinfectant or a 1:10 bleach solution, as taught in training.

Caregivers do not recap, bend, or break needles, do not pick up sharps with bare hands, and do not place sharps in household trash. If a client's sharps are found, the caregiver uses tongs or a brush and dustpan, places them in a rigid puncture-resistant container, and tells the PCA supervisor. Caregivers do not perform tasks involving sharps.
After an exposure incident, the employee immediately washes the area with soap and water (or flushes eyes, nose, or mouth with water), then calls the PCA supervisor at [PHONE] right away.

The PCA supervisor arranges, the same day, a confidential medical evaluation by a licensed health care professional at [CLINIC NAME AND ADDRESS], at no cost to the employee, including documentation of the route of exposure and circumstances, source individual identification where possible, testing consent, and counseling.

The agency gives the health care professional a copy of 29 CFR 1910.1030, a description of the employee's duties, the exposure report, and relevant vaccination records. The agency obtains the professional's written opinion within 15 days after the evaluation and gives a copy to the employee within that time.
The PCA supervisor completes an incident report under SAF-02 within 24 hours and records the exposure on the sharps injury log if a contaminated sharp was involved, protecting the employee's privacy.

The Administrator keeps confidential medical records for each employee with occupational exposure for the duration of employment plus 30 years, and training records for 3 years. These records are kept separate from the general personnel file (PER-13) and released only as the standard permits.
The Administrator reviews each exposure incident through the quality assurance program (GOV-05) to determine whether engineering controls, training, or supplies should change.

responsibilities.duty: Completes the exposure determination, maintains the exposure control plan, ensures vaccine, PPE, training and recordkeeping.
Responds to exposure reports, arranges post-exposure evaluation, completes incident reporting.
Uses universal precautions and PPE, avoids sharps, and reports any exposure immediately.
Provides vaccination, post-exposure evaluation and the written opinion.

documentation: Written exposure determination
Written exposure control plan with annual review date
Hepatitis B vaccination records or signed declination forms
Bloodborne pathogens training records (date, content, trainer, attendees)
Post-exposure evaluation records and health care professional's written opinion
Sharps injury log (if applicable)
Incident report (SAF-02)

policies.title: Client Emergency and Disaster Plans
policies.applies_to: All clients, caregivers, PCA supervisors, scheduler and on-call staff; all programs
policies.purpose: To ensure each client has an individual emergency plan, that care continues or is safely arranged during severe weather and disasters, and that staff know what to do in an emergency.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] identifies each client's emergency contacts, evacuation needs and medical vulnerabilities at intake and records them in the client's person-centered service plan, consistent with OAC 5160-44-02 (citation C37), which requires that the plan include back-up plans and be reviewed at least every 12 months, on significant change, or on request. The agency's back-up plan under OAC 173-39-02.11(C)(2) (citation C24) applies during severe weather and disasters, so a PCA and an RN or LPN supervisor remain available during scheduled hours. The agency tests its on-call line on a regular schedule. Staff orientation covers emergency procedures (OAC 173-39-02.11(C)(3)(b)(vi)). In a life-threatening emergency, staff call 911 first.

definitions.definition: The part of the client's service plan that lists emergency contacts, evacuation needs, medical vulnerabilities, preferred hospital, and arrangements if care cannot be delivered.
A condition that makes a client especially at risk during an emergency, such as oxygen use, powered medical equipment, limited mobility, dementia, or dependence on refrigerated medication.
The agency telephone number, [PHONE], answered 24 hours a day by a qualified on-call supervisor.
The agency's written arrangement for providing a replacement PCA or supervisor, or for alerting the client's contacts, when scheduled staff are unavailable (SVC-08).

procedures: At intake and assessment (SVC-02), the PCA supervisor asks the client or representative to name emergency contacts (at least two), the preferred hospital, physician, pharmacy, and any person who would assist in an evacuation. The client leads this conversation.

The PCA supervisor identifies evacuation needs (mobility aids, need for hands-on help, pets, service animals), medical vulnerabilities (oxygen, powered equipment, medications needing refrigeration), communication needs, and language needs, and writes them in plain language in the service plan (SVC-03).

The plan states what the caregiver should do in a fire, medical emergency, severe weather, power loss, and evacuation, and what the client prefers. The client or representative signs the plan and receives a copy.
The emergency information is placed in the client's chart and a summary is placed in the client's home copy of the plan so the caregiver can see it at the start of each visit.
The PCA supervisor reviews the emergency plan at least every 12 months, when the client's condition or living situation changes significantly, and whenever the client asks.

During orientation (PER-09) and annual in-service (PER-11), staff are trained on emergency procedures: calling 911, basic first aid within scope, fire safety, evacuation assistance, severe weather shelter, and who to call at the agency.

In an emergency in the home, the caregiver calls 911 first when there is risk to life or safety, stays with the client as safely as possible, then calls the on-call line at [PHONE] and the client's emergency contact. Incidents are documented under SAF-02 and SVC-10.

When severe weather or a disaster is forecast or occurring, the Administrator or on-call supervisor decides whether to operate normal schedules. The decision is based on National Weather Service warnings, local emergency declarations and road conditions, and is documented.

Before or during a severe weather or disaster event, the scheduler calls every client identified in the plan as medically vulnerable, and then other clients, to confirm safety, any needed rescheduling, and the contact who will check on them. Calls are logged.

Caregivers do not put themselves in danger traveling in hazardous conditions. A caregiver who cannot reach a client calls the on-call line, and the scheduler activates the back-up plan under SVC-08 and tries the client's emergency contact.
If a client's authorized care cannot be provided, the PCA supervisor notifies the client's case manager or care coordinator promptly and reports under SVC-14 and REC-02 as applicable.

The agency tests the on-call line at least quarterly by placing a call at a random hour, confirming the on-call supervisor responds within 15 minutes, and recording the result. Failures are corrected immediately and reviewed under GOV-05.
After a disaster or significant emergency, the Administrator holds a review within 30 days, updates this policy and client plans as needed, and records the review.
The agency keeps a current list of on-call supervisors, back-up caregivers, and local emergency management and utility numbers at the business site and in the on-call phone.

responsibilities.duty: Approves severe weather decisions, assures on-call coverage, and reviews tests and events.
Builds and updates client emergency plans, trains staff, and responds to on-call calls.
Contacts clients during events, activates the back-up plan, and logs calls.
Knows the client's emergency plan, calls 911 when needed, and reports to the agency.

documentation: Emergency section of each client service plan, with signature and distribution record
On-call line test log
Severe weather and disaster decision log and client call log
Orientation and in-service records covering emergency procedures
Incident reports and post-event review notes

policies.title: Caregiver Safety in the Home and Workplace Violence
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, PCA supervisors, and office staff who visit client homes; all programs
policies.purpose: To protect caregivers from violence, threats and unsafe conditions in client homes and the workplace, and to ensure that incidents are reported and acted upon.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not tolerate violence, threats or harassment against staff, and staff safety is a condition of service. Staff may leave an unsafe home and must notify the supervisor immediately. Staff report firearms, hostile persons and unsafe conditions to the supervisor. Threats and safety concerns are reported to the Ohio Department of Medicaid (ODM) or its designee within 24 hours as required by OAC 5160-44-31 (citation C32) for Medicaid waiver services. Each incident is documented under SAF-02. Staff conduct standards, including that staff must not use alcohol or drugs, be distracted, or allow visitors while working, are consistent with OAC 173-39-02(B) (citation C20) and PER-15. Staff must always be at least 18 years old (C32). No staff member is penalized for leaving an unsafe situation in good faith.

definitions.definition: Any act or threat of physical violence, harassment, intimidation, or other threatening behavior against a staff member in a client's home, at the business site, or while traveling for work.

A hazard in the client's home that creates a reasonable risk of injury, such as an intoxicated or hostile person, an unsecured weapon, a violent pet, active drug use, structural hazards, no working heat in extreme cold, or an infestation.
The entity ODM designates to receive reports, such as the client's case management agency or the contact named in the client's waiver enrollment.

procedures: During intake and assessment (SVC-02), the PCA supervisor completes a home safety assessment by asking the client about firearms, pets, other household members with a history of violence or threats, smoking, hazards, and the neighborhood, and records the answers in the client record.
The PCA supervisor shares relevant safety information with the assigned caregiver before the first visit, and reviews it again after any change in the household.

During orientation (PER-09) the agency trains caregivers to recognize warning signs, de-escalate, safely leave a home, protect personal information, and use the on-call line at [PHONE]. Caregivers do not carry weapons while working.

A caregiver who feels threatened or sees an unsafe condition may leave immediately. The caregiver calls 911 if there is imminent danger, and then calls the PCA supervisor or on-call line right away from a safe location.

Caregivers report to the PCA supervisor, as soon as they see them, any firearm that is not locked or unloaded, any hostile person, active substance use, or any other unsafe condition. Caregivers do not handle or move firearms.
The caregiver's report is made by telephone at once and followed by a written incident report within 24 hours using the SAF-02 form.

The PCA supervisor interviews the caregiver, checks on the caregiver's well-being, and arranges for the caregiver to be reassigned or relieved immediately if needed. The scheduler arranges coverage or notifies the client's contacts under SVC-08 so the client's safety is not compromised.

The PCA supervisor or Administrator contacts the client or representative to discuss the incident and attempts to resolve it. For clients with a case manager, the Administrator informs the case manager at the same time.

For clients served through Medicaid waiver programs, the Administrator reports the threat or safety concern to ODM or its designee within 24 hours of learning of it, and records the date, time, person contacted, and information provided.

If the unsafe situation cannot be corrected, the Administrator may suspend visits or discontinue services under SVC-11, with proper notice to the client, case manager and payer, after confirming the client's immediate safety needs are met.
Suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation of the client discovered during an event is reported under SAF-01 in addition to this policy.
The agency offers support to staff after an incident, such as time off, referral to employee assistance resources, and reporting to law enforcement if the employee chooses.
Retaliation against any staff who reports a safety concern or leaves an unsafe home in good faith is prohibited and is itself a violation of PER-15.
The Administrator reviews all workplace violence and safety incidents quarterly through GOV-05, and updates training and assessment tools as needed.

responsibilities.duty: Makes 24-hour reports to ODM or its designee, decides on suspension of service, and reviews incidents.
Completes home safety assessments, receives reports, supports the caregiver, and coordinates with the client.
Arranges coverage and logs calls.
Leaves unsafe situations, reports hazards immediately, and completes an incident report.

documentation: Home safety assessment in the client record
Incident report (SAF-02) for every threat, assault or unsafe condition
Record of the 24-hour report to ODM or its designee
Orientation and in-service records on safety and de-escalation
Quarterly QA review notes

policies.title: Transporting Clients
policies.applies_to: All caregivers who drive in the course of duties; clients receiving errands under a service plan; all programs
policies.purpose: To set safe conditions for errands and any client transportation so clients and staff are protected and services stay within the authorized service plan.
policies.policy: Errands are covered when authorized in the client's service plan; OAC 173-39-02.11(A)-(B) (citation C23) lists homemaker tasks and errands among personal care services authorized in the service plan. Transporting a client in a caregiver's or the agency's vehicle requires specific written authorization in the service plan. A caregiver who drives must hold a valid Ohio driver's license and automobile insurance, and the agency carries hired and non-owned auto coverage. Staff may not take a client to the business site (OAC 173-39-02(B)(8)). Where a payer program does not allow transportation, [AGENCY NAME] does not provide it for that client. Caregivers never drive a client while impaired, distracted, or unlicensed.

definitions.definition: A task such as shopping, picking up a prescription, or mailing items, done for the client as authorized in the service plan.
Carrying a client in a motor vehicle to a destination such as a medical appointment, pharmacy, or store.
Liability insurance that covers the agency when employees drive their own or rented vehicles on agency business.

procedures: During assessment (SVC-02), the PCA supervisor asks whether the client needs errands or transport, and if so, documents the destinations, frequency, and the client's mobility needs.

Errands and any transportation are added to the service plan only if the payer program permits them and the plan states the type, frequency and limits. Transport requires written authorization in the plan, signed by the client or representative (SVC-03). The authorization is documented before the first trip.

The scheduler assigns transport only to a caregiver who has a valid driver's license and current auto insurance on file. The office verifies the license and insurance before the first transport and again at each renewal date.
The office confirms the agency's hired and non-owned auto coverage is in force and includes the staff driver (GOV-08). The Administrator keeps the certificate of insurance on file.

Staff who drive for the agency complete a motor vehicle record check at hire and annually, and disclose any suspension, loss of license, or change in insurance within one business day. Any caregiver whose driving privileges are lost may not drive for the agency.

Before every trip, the caregiver confirms that the client is able to travel, wears a seat belt, and sits in a seat suited to the client's mobility. Car seats are used for children, as required by law.
Caregivers do not transport clients in wheelchairs that cannot be properly secured, do not lift clients beyond their training, and call the office if a client's condition makes travel unsafe.
Caregivers use hands-free or no phone, obey traffic laws, do not smoke or drink alcohol, and do not use impairing substances before or during driving (consistent with PER-15).
Errands are completed using the client's money or funds only as allowed under CR-04. The caregiver keeps receipts, records change, and obtains the client's signature on the errand log.
Staff do not take a client to the agency's business site (OAC 173-39-02(B)(8)) or to the caregiver's home, and do not make personal stops while the client is in the vehicle.
The caregiver records each trip with the date, start and end time, mileage, and destination in the visit documentation, and in EVV as required (SVC-09).
If an accident, injury, or other emergency occurs, the caregiver calls 911 if needed, then the on-call supervisor at [PHONE]. The caregiver completes an incident report under SAF-02 within 24 hours.
The Administrator reviews transportation events, complaints, and insurance status at least quarterly (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains insurance coverage, reviews driver records, and approves transport policies.
Includes errands and transport in the service plan only with authorization and checks safety needs.
Assigns transport only to verified drivers.
Drives safely, holds a valid license and insurance, and documents all trips.

documentation: Service plan section authorizing errands and transport, signed by the client or representative
Copy of each driver's license, insurance and annual motor vehicle record check
Certificate of hired and non-owned auto insurance
Errand log, receipts and trip log
Incident reports (SAF-02)

policies.title: Caregiver Qualifications and Certification
policies.applies_to: All personal care aides (PCAs) and prospective PCAs; ODA PASSPORT personal care, ODM Ohio Home Care Waiver, Older Americans Act personal care, and private pay
policies.purpose: To ensure every caregiver meets the qualifications Ohio requires before delivering personal care to any client.
policies.policy: This policy meets OAC 173-39-02.11(C)(3)(a) — PCA initial qualifications (citation C25). [AGENCY NAME] does not allow any individual to provide personal care until the Administrator verifies that the individual meets at least one of the following qualifications: (i) the individual is a state-tested nurse aide (STNA); (ii) the individual meets the Medicare home health aide standards; (iii) the individual has one year of previous supervised aide experience plus a competency evaluation; (iv) the individual has completed the Community Alternatives Level of Assistance (COALA) program or a vocational program; or (v) the individual has completed another program of at least 30 hours covering the topics listed in OAC 173-39-02.11(C)(3)(a)(v)(b)(i)-(x). All staff must be age 18 or older (OAC 5160-44-31). For the ODM Ohio Home Care Waiver, agency aides must be employed by a Medicare-certified or accredited agency and must hold an ODH or Medicare competency certificate and first aid training (citation C30). For Older Americans Act personal care, the agency applies the aide qualifications and 6-hour in-service standard in citation C38. The Administrator confirms the current text of the ODA rule, including any change to the 30-hour requirement, at each annual policy review (GOV-04).

definitions.definition: A personal care aide who provides hands-on assistance with activities of daily living, instrumental activities of daily living, home management, homemaker tasks and errands, and help with self-administration of medications, as authorized in the service plan.
A state-tested nurse aide listed as active and in good standing on the Ohio Nurse Aide Registry.
The federal training and competency standards for home health aides, evidenced by a certificate of completion and competency.
The Community Alternatives Level of Assistance program, one of the recognized completion paths in the ODA rule.
A documented assessment by a registered nurse that the individual can safely perform the personal care tasks required for the job.

procedures: Before offering employment, the Administrator or hiring manager tells every applicant in writing the minimum qualifications, and verifies the applicant's age (18 or older) from government-issued identification.

Qualification (i), STNA: the office prints the applicant's Ohio Nurse Aide Registry record, confirms active status and no findings of abuse, neglect or misappropriation, and places the printout in the personnel file.

Qualification (ii), Medicare home health aide standards: the office obtains a copy of the training certificate and competency evaluation showing completion of a program meeting the Medicare standards, verifies with the issuer, and files it.

Qualification (iii), previous experience: the office obtains written proof of at least one year of supervised aide experience, such as a signed statement from the prior employer or employment records, and the PCA supervisor completes and documents a competency evaluation of the applicant's skills (PER-10).
Qualification (iv), COALA or vocational program: the office obtains the completion certificate or transcript and verifies it with the issuer.

Qualification (v), other program: the office obtains the certificate and course outline, and the PCA supervisor confirms the program was at least 30 hours and covered every topic in OAC 173-39-02.11(C)(3)(a)(v)(b)(i)-(x). If a topic is missing or hours are short, the applicant completes the missing training with the agency before client contact, and the content and hours are recorded.

The Administrator signs and dates a qualification verification form for each PCA that identifies the qualification relied on, the documents reviewed, and the reviewer. No client assignment is made without this signed form (PER-02).

The office confirms that the background check requirements are met under PER-04 through PER-08 before an individual provides care, and that the individual has no disqualifying finding on the Nurse Aide Registry or other required registries.

For Ohio Home Care Waiver clients, the Administrator assigns an aide only if the agency itself meets the program's employer condition (Medicare-certified or accredited agency) and the aide holds an ODH or Medicare competency certificate and current first aid certification; copies are kept in the personnel file. If the agency does not meet that condition, it does not offer Waiver aide services (SVC-13).

For Older Americans Act personal care, the Administrator verifies that the aide meets the same qualification standards and completes the required 6 hours of ODA-approved in-service per 12 months (PER-11).
The agency also confirms that each aide completes orientation before any in-person client contact (PER-09) and in-service training each 12 months (PER-11).

The PCA supervisor reviews the qualification file for completeness within the first week of employment, and the Administrator audits all qualification files at least annually and before each license or certification renewal.

If a qualification expires, is revoked, or cannot be verified, the Administrator removes the PCA from client assignments the same day, informs the scheduler to arrange coverage under SVC-08, and documents the action.
The Administrator reviews this policy at least annually and when ODA or ODM revises its rules, including any ODA change to the 30-hour program requirement.

responsibilities.duty: Verifies qualifications, signs the verification form, and audits files annually.
Conducts competency evaluations and reviews training content against the rule.
Obtains registry printouts, certificates and proof of experience, and maintains files.
Assigns only verified PCAs to clients.

documentation: Qualification verification form signed by the Administrator for each PCA
Ohio Nurse Aide Registry printout, certificates, transcripts, or proof of prior supervised experience
Competency evaluation record (PER-10)
Proof of age (18 or older)
For Ohio Home Care Waiver aides: ODH or Medicare competency certificate and first aid certificate
Annual file audit record

policies.title: Verification and Records of PCA Qualifications
policies.applies_to: All personal care aide (PCA) applicants and employees, the PCA Supervisor, and the personnel record keeper of [AGENCY NAME], for ODA PASSPORT personal care and any other service where PCA qualifications must be shown.
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] can prove, from its own files and at any time, how each PCA meets the qualification requirements before the PCA has in-person contact with a client, and to keep those proofs for the required period.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] will verify and document how every PCA meets the qualifications in OAC 173-39-02.11(C)(3) before the PCA is scheduled for any in-person client contact. This policy meets OAC 173-39-02.11(C)(3)(f)(i)-(iii) (Verification of PCA qualifications) and OAC 173-39-02.11(C)(5)(b) (Retaining records on how each PCA meets the qualifications in paragraph (C)(3)).

Verification of PCA qualifications, item C(3)(f): for each PCA the agency will keep (i) a certificate of completion of the qualifying training or, if no certificate exists, a written record of the school or organization, course name, dates and hours; (ii) for a State Tested Nursing Assistant (STNA), the Ohio nurse aide registry search results; and (iii) for a PCA qualifying through the experience pathway, the records of previous employment that show the experience.

Records of how each PCA meets (C)(3), item C(5)(b): this is the agency's written policy on keeping those records. The agency keeps one qualification record for each PCA that shows which pathway was used and holds the supporting proof. Qualification records are kept for the length of employment plus 6 years. A PCA with no complete qualification record will not be scheduled for client contact. Orientation, in-service and verification records under OAC 173-39-02.11(C)(3)(b)-(f) are kept in the same file (see PER-09 and PER-11).

definitions.definition: A personal care aide employed by [AGENCY NAME] who provides nonmedical personal care to clients.
State Tested Nursing Assistant, listed on the Ohio nurse aide registry.

The way a PCA meets OAC 173-39-02.11(C)(3): completed training (shown by certificate or course record), STNA status (shown by registry search), or prior work experience (shown by previous-employment records).
The file section for one PCA that holds the proofs in this policy and the checklist showing which pathway the PCA met.

procedures: The Administrator or designee reviews each PCA application and identifies which qualification pathway the applicant claims (training, STNA, or experience) before an offer of client-contact work.
For a training pathway, the PCA supervisor or designee obtains the original or a copy of the certificate of completion and places it in the qualification record.

If no certificate exists, the designee records in writing the school or organization, the course name, the dates and the hours, and obtains the applicant's signature on the record. The designee then confirms the details with the school or organization where possible and notes the date, method and name of the person contacted.

For an STNA, the designee runs a search of the Ohio nurse aide registry, prints or saves the results showing the date of search, and files the result in the qualification record. The search is also used for the database review in PER-04.

For the experience pathway, the designee obtains previous-employment records (such as written verification from the prior employer showing employer name, dates and duties). The designee files them and records who reviewed them and on what date.

The reviewer completes the Qualification Verification Checklist, which names the pathway met, lists each document received, and is signed and dated by the reviewer and the Administrator or PCA Supervisor.
No PCA is placed on the schedule for in-person client contact until the checklist is complete and signed. The scheduler checks for the 'Qualification Verified' mark before assigning any PCA.

If a document is missing, illegible or does not match the claimed pathway, the designee notifies the applicant in writing within 2 business days, states what is needed, and holds the PCA from client contact until it is received.

The agency keeps orientation completion records (see PER-09) and annual in-service certificates (see PER-11) in the same qualification record, so a single review shows the PCA's complete training status.

The designee reviews every active PCA's qualification record at least once a year and at each supervisory visit cycle to make sure no item has been removed or is incomplete. Gaps are corrected within 14 days or the PCA is removed from client contact until corrected.

Qualification records are stored in the locked personnel files (or access-controlled electronic files) described in PER-13 and REC-03 and are available to ODA, ODM, ODH and the case management agency on request.
Records are kept for the whole period of employment and for 6 years after the PCA's employment ends. Destruction after that period is authorized in writing by the Administrator and logged.
The Administrator reviews qualification-record completeness as part of the quality review in GOV-05 and reports findings to the governing body.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures this policy is carried out, signs off the checklist or delegates it in writing, and authorizes record destruction after the retention period.
Reviews qualification proofs, completes the checklist, and conducts the annual record review.
Collects and files the proofs, runs registry searches, and keeps records secure and retrievable.
Does not schedule any PCA who lacks a verified qualification record.
Provides accurate certificates, course information and employment history and tells the agency of any change.

documentation: Qualification Verification Checklist for each PCA, signed and dated
Certificates of completion, or written record of school or organization, course name, dates and hours
Ohio nurse aide registry search results (for STNAs), with search date
Previous-employment records (for the experience pathway)
Orientation and in-service certificates and records
Annual qualification-record review log
Records destruction log (after employment plus 6 years)

policies.title: Job Descriptions
policies.applies_to: All positions at [AGENCY NAME]: Administrator, PCA Supervisor, Scheduler and Personal Care Aide (PCA), and any other position the agency creates.
policies.purpose: To define in writing what each position does and does not do, so that staff know their duties, caregivers stay within the nonmedical scope, and the agency can show reviewers that duties and qualifications are clear.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] maintains a written job description for every position. This policy meets OAC 173-39-02.11(C)(5)(a) (Job descriptions for each position).

Each job description will state the position title, the person to whom the position reports, the minimum qualifications, the duties and the limits on duties. The Administrator, PCA Supervisor, Scheduler and PCA each have their own description.

PCA job descriptions list only tasks within the nonmedical scope in SVC-01 and state that the PCA may not perform tasks outside that scope. The PCA Supervisor description requires an active Ohio RN or LPN license (see SVC-05). Each description requires staff to meet the conduct standards in PER-15, as required by the ODA provider written-policy requirement for staff conduct. Every employee signs a receipt for his or her job description at hire and on every revision.

definitions.definition: A written document that sets out a position's title, reporting line, qualifications, duties, limits and conduct requirements.
The personal care, homemaker and related tasks that [AGENCY NAME] permits caregivers to perform, as defined in SVC-01.
A signed and dated acknowledgment by the employee that he or she has received and understands the job description.
