procedures: The Administrator writes or approves a job description for each position before the position is filled, using the agency's standard format.

Each description includes: title, reporting line, minimum qualifications, essential duties, limits on duties, required training, and the statement that the employee must follow the agency's conduct standards (PER-15) and client rights (CR-01).

The PCA description lists only nonmedical tasks consistent with SVC-01, such as personal care, mobility help, meal preparation, light housekeeping, and reminders and assistance consistent with SVC-06. It states that the PCA may not perform nursing tasks, injections, wound care or other tasks outside the scope, unless authorized under an applicable program rule and the agency's policies.

The PCA Supervisor description requires an active, unencumbered Ohio RN or LPN license, describes supervisory visits (SVC-04), service plan duties (SVC-03) and back-up duties (SVC-08), and requires the supervisor to verify the license through the Ohio licensing board before hire (see SVC-05).
The Scheduler description covers scheduling, missed-visit handling (SVC-07), EVV oversight (SVC-09) and confidentiality, and states that the scheduler may not assign tasks outside the service plan.
The Administrator description covers the responsibilities in GOV-01, including oversight of licensure, personnel and records.
Before the first day of work, the hiring manager gives the new employee the job description and reviews it with him or her. The employee signs and dates the receipt.
The signed receipt is filed in the personnel record (PER-13) within 3 business days.

When a job description is revised, the Administrator approves the change, the revision date and version are recorded under GOV-04, and each affected employee gets the new description and signs a new receipt within 14 days.
The Administrator reviews all job descriptions at least annually and when scope, program rules or staffing change, and records the review date.
The PCA Supervisor uses the PCA job description as the standard when conducting supervisory visits and performance evaluations.
Current job descriptions are kept available at the business site for review by ODH, ODA, ODM and case management agency staff (see REC-03).

responsibilities.duty: Approves all job descriptions, reviews them annually and ensures every employee has a signed receipt.
Reviews the PCA description with each new PCA and uses it in supervision.
Delivers the description at hire, obtains the signed receipt and files it.
Perform duties within their job description and sign the receipt at hire and on revisions.

documentation: Current job description for each position (version and date)
Signed job description receipts at hire and on each revision
Annual job description review record
Document control log entries (GOV-04)

policies.title: Background Checks and Employee Registries (Written Criminal Records Check Policy)
policies.applies_to: All applicants and employees of [AGENCY NAME] in direct-care positions, and the Administrator or designee who conducts the checks.
policies.purpose: To state the agency's written criminal records check policy, as required for the ODH nonmedical license application, and to make sure no one who is barred from direct care is employed in a direct-care position.
policies.policy:
This is the written criminal records check policy of [AGENCY NAME] and is submitted with the ODH nonmedical home health services license application. It meets OAC 3701-60-03(B)(3)(g) (a copy of the home health agency's written criminal records check policy), as required by ORC 3740.03(B) and OAC 3701-60-03(B).

[AGENCY NAME] will not employ, or continue to employ, a person in a direct-care position if that person appears in a database listed below or has a disqualifying offense under ORC 3740.11. Disqualifying information bars employment in direct care.

Every direct-care applicant is screened before first client contact. Before the criminal records check is requested, the agency reviews each of the following for the applicant and for each current employee: (1) the federal System for Award Management (SAM) exclusion list; (2) the HHS Office of Inspector General List of Excluded Individuals/Entities (OIG LEIE); (3) the Ohio Department of Developmental Disabilities (DODD) abuse registry; (4) the sex offender database; (5) the Ohio Department of Rehabilitation and Correction (ODRC) inmate database; and (6) the Ohio nurse aide registry.

The agency then requests a criminal records check from the Bureau of Criminal Identification and Investigation (BCI) under PER-05, and handles rechecks, FBI requests, fees and exceptions under PER-06 and PER-07. Conditional employment and disqualifying offenses are handled under PER-08. Criminal records check reports are confidential and are not shared except as the law permits.

definitions.definition: A position at [AGENCY NAME] in which the employee has in-person contact with clients or access to clients' records, property or funds in the course of providing care.
The check of SAM, OIG LEIE, the DODD abuse registry, the sex offender database, the ODRC inmate database and the Ohio nurse aide registry, performed before the criminal records check.
The Ohio Bureau of Criminal Identification and Investigation, which conducts the criminal records check on request.
A listing in one of the databases, or a disqualifying offense under ORC 3740.11, that bars employment in direct care.

procedures: The Administrator designates in writing the person ([NAME AND TITLE OF DESIGNEE]) who conducts database reviews and requests criminal records checks. The designee must keep the results confidential.
At application, the designee tells the applicant that employment in direct care depends on a database review and a criminal records check, and gives the applicant a copy of this policy.

Before requesting the criminal records check, the designee reviews all six databases (SAM, OIG LEIE, DODD abuse registry, sex offender database, ODRC inmate database, Ohio nurse aide registry) for the applicant. The designee prints or saves each result showing the date, the name searched and the reviewer's name.

If any database shows disqualifying information, the designee stops the hiring process, notifies the Administrator the same day, and the agency does not employ the applicant in a direct-care position.
If the databases show no disqualifying information, the designee follows PER-05 to request the BCI criminal records check, and PER-06 and PER-07 for FBI information, fees and exceptions.

No applicant has client contact until the database review is complete and clear and the check has been requested and the applicant is eligible for conditional employment under PER-08, or the report has been received showing no disqualifying offense.

When the BCI report is received, the designee reviews it, records the result on the Background Screening Checklist, and gives it to the Administrator for a hire or no-hire decision. Any disqualifying offense results in no employment in direct care (PER-08).

The same database review is repeated for every current direct-care employee at the time of each five-year recheck (PER-06), and as agency practice at least annually, and whenever the agency receives information suggesting a listing.

If a current employee is found to appear in a database or to have a disqualifying offense, the Administrator removes the employee from client contact immediately, ends direct-care employment, and documents the action.

Reports, database printouts and results are kept in a separate, locked background-check file (or access-controlled electronic file), not in the general personnel file. Only the Administrator and designee may access them, plus regulators who are entitled to review them.
The agency does not disclose criminal records check reports to anyone except as permitted by law, and does not copy or forward them for any other purpose.

The Administrator audits all direct-care background files at least annually to confirm that each has complete database reviews and a check on file, and reports results to the governing body under GOV-05. Corrections are made within 5 business days.

responsibilities.duty: Owns this policy, makes final hiring decisions, removes any person who is barred, and conducts the annual audit.
Performs database reviews, requests BCI checks, and keeps reports confidential and filed.
Does not schedule any person for client contact until cleared under this policy.
Provide accurate information, sign the required forms and complete fingerprinting.

documentation: Database review printouts or screenshots (six databases) with date and reviewer name
BCI criminal records check requests and reports (confidential file)
Background Screening Checklist for each employee
Applicant notice acknowledgment (PER-05)
Annual background file audit record
Copy of this policy submitted with the ODH license application

policies.title: Criminal Records Check Procedure: BCI Requests, Notice and Forms
policies.applies_to: The Administrator and designee, and all applicants and employees for direct-care positions at [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To set the step-by-step procedure for requesting a BCI criminal records check, notifying applicants, handling the prescribed forms and fingerprints, and refusing employment to anyone who does not complete the process.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] will request a criminal records check from the Bureau of Criminal Identification and Investigation (BCI) for every applicant for a direct-care position, as required by ORC 3740.11 and OAC 3701-60-06. The requirements below are tied to the official items in OAC 3701-60-06:

- OAC 3701-60-06(A) (Request for check): the chief administrator or designee requests that the superintendent of BCI conduct a criminal records check on each applicant for a direct-care position.
- OAC 3701-60-06(D) (Notification): the agency notifies the applicant or employee that fingerprint impressions are required and that a criminal records check will be conducted. The notice also covers any fee under OAC 3701-60-06(E)(2) and any fingerprinting fee authorized under ORC 109.572(C)(2).
- OAC 3701-60-06(F) (Forms): the agency provides the prescribed forms and the fingerprint impression sheet or instructions, obtains the completed forms, and forwards them to the superintendent.
- OAC 3701-60-06(G) (Failure to complete): an applicant or employee who fails to complete the forms or provide fingerprint impressions will not be employed in any position for which a check is required.

The database review required by PER-04 is completed before the request is made. Reports are confidential.

definitions.definition: The superintendent of the Ohio Bureau of Criminal Identification and Investigation (BCI).
The criminal records check request forms and fingerprint impression sheet, or instructions for electronic fingerprinting, that BCI requires.
The person named in writing by the Administrator to carry out criminal records check duties.

procedures: After the database review in PER-04 shows no disqualifying information, the Administrator or designee decides to proceed with the applicant and requests the criminal records check on the same business day or the next.

Before fingerprinting, the designee gives the applicant the written Criminal Records Check Notice. It states that fingerprint impressions are required, that a criminal records check will be conducted, the amount of any fee the applicant may be charged, and any fingerprinting fees authorized under ORC 109.572(C)(2). Fee rules are in PER-07.
The applicant signs and dates the notice. The designee keeps the signed copy in the background-check file and gives the applicant a copy.

The designee provides the applicant with the prescribed BCI forms and the fingerprint impression sheet, or instructions for electronic fingerprinting at an approved location, and explains how to complete them.
The designee reviews each form for completeness (name, identifiers, signature and date) before it is submitted and returns any incomplete form to the applicant the same day.
The designee forwards the completed forms and fingerprints to the superintendent in the manner BCI requires, and records the date requested and the method used.
If the applicant is to be conditionally employed, the Administrator confirms that the request was made within the timeframe in PER-08 before any client contact is permitted.

If an applicant or employee does not complete the forms or does not provide fingerprint impressions (including by failing to attend fingerprinting after a reasonable written request with a deadline of [NUMBER] business days), the designee notifies the Administrator, and the person is not employed in any direct-care position.

If fingerprints are rejected as unreadable, the designee gives the applicant written notice within 2 business days and helps arrange new fingerprinting. The person remains subject to PER-08 during this time.
When BCI returns the report, the designee reviews it for disqualifying offenses, records the date received and the result, and gives it to the Administrator for a decision under PER-04 and PER-08.
All forms, notices, fingerprint records and BCI reports are filed in the confidential background-check file and are not placed in the general personnel record or shared with anyone without authority.
The Administrator checks a sample of files every quarter to confirm each applicant received the notice, signed forms and a documented request date.

responsibilities.duty: Requests, or authorizes the designee to request, the criminal records check and makes the final employment decision.
Gives notice, provides forms, forwards completed forms to BCI and keeps records.
Completes the forms and provides fingerprint impressions by the stated deadline.

documentation: Signed Criminal Records Check Notice (fingerprints, fees, ORC 109.572(C)(2) fingerprint fees)
Completed BCI forms and fingerprint sheet, or electronic fingerprinting receipt
Request log with date, method and person who submitted
BCI report with date received and review sign-off (confidential)
Written notice to an applicant who did not complete the process
Quarterly sample audit record

policies.title: Five-Year Rechecks and FBI Residency Requirements
policies.applies_to: All direct-care employees and applicants of [AGENCY NAME], and the Administrator and designee who schedule and request the checks.
policies.purpose: To make sure direct-care employees are rechecked on time and that applicants who have not lived in Ohio for five years, or lack a recent FBI check, are also checked at the federal level.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] will conduct a criminal background check of each direct-care employee on a recurring basis and will request FBI information when the residency requirement is not met, as required by OAC 3701-60-06.

This policy meets OAC 3701-60-06(B) (Rechecks): the chief administrator or designee conducts a criminal background check on direct-care employees. For employees hired before 1/1/2008, the check is done no later than 30 days after the anniversary of the hire date and at least every five years. For employees hired on or after 1/1/2008, the check is done no later than 30 days after the fifth anniversary of the hire date and at least every five years.

This policy meets OAC 3701-60-06(C) (Residency requirement): if the applicant cannot show five years of Ohio residency, or an FBI check within that period, the chief administrator requests that the superintendent obtain FBI information. The agency may request FBI information even if the applicant does meet the residency requirement.

The database review in PER-04 is repeated at each recheck. Anyone with a disqualifying result is removed from direct care under PER-08.

definitions.definition: A new BCI criminal records check of a current direct-care employee, done on the five-year schedule in this policy.
The yearly date matching the employee's date of hire. The fifth anniversary is the date five years after hire.
National criminal history information obtained through the BCI superintendent.
Five years of Ohio residency, or proof of an FBI check within the five-year period.

procedures: At hire, the designee records each direct-care employee's date of hire and the date of the last criminal records check in a Recheck Tracking Log.

The designee calculates the recheck due date for each employee. For employees hired on or after 1/1/2008, the due date is 30 days after the fifth hire anniversary, and then at least every five years after each completed check. For employees hired before 1/1/2008, the due date is 30 days after the anniversary of the hire date and at least every five years.
The designee reviews the tracking log monthly and flags every employee whose recheck falls due within the next 90 days.
At least 60 days before the due date, the designee gives the employee the written notice and forms under PER-05, so fingerprinting can be completed well before the deadline.
The designee repeats the six-database review in PER-04 and files the new results before or at the time the recheck is requested.
The designee requests the recheck from BCI no later than the due date and records the date requested and the date results are received.

At application, the designee asks each applicant to state in writing where he or she has lived for the past five years and to give proof of Ohio residency where available (for example, a driver license or lease), and records the answer.

If the applicant cannot show five years of Ohio residency, or an FBI check within the past five years, the Administrator requests that the BCI superintendent obtain FBI information as part of the check, and the applicant is notified of this under PER-05 and of any fees under PER-07.

If the applicant does meet the residency requirement, the Administrator may still request FBI information. The Administrator records the reason when this is done (for example, a gap in residency history or an inconsistency in the application).

If an employee does not complete forms or fingerprinting for a recheck by the due date, the designee notifies the Administrator, and the employee is removed from direct-care duties until the process is completed. PER-05 applies.
A recheck result with a disqualifying offense is handled under PER-08. The Administrator documents the date of removal and any report required under REC-02.
The Administrator reviews the Recheck Tracking Log quarterly. Any overdue recheck is reported to the governing body and corrected within 5 business days.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures rechecks are timely, requests FBI information when required, and removes employees when a recheck is not completed or shows disqualifying information.
Maintains the tracking log, gives notice, completes the database reviews and submits requests.
Completes forms and fingerprints when asked and reports any arrest or conviction as required by PER-15.

documentation: Recheck Tracking Log (hire date, last check, due date, request date, result date)
Written residency statement and proof for each applicant
Request for FBI information and its date
New database review printouts at each recheck
BCI results (confidential file)
Quarterly review record

policies.title: BCI Fees, Reverification and Employment-Service Exception
policies.applies_to: The Administrator and designee of [AGENCY NAME], and applicants and employees in direct-care positions who are subject to criminal records checks.
policies.purpose: To explain who pays for criminal records checks, when a recent check can be reverified and accepted, and when a new check is not needed for an applicant referred by an employment service.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] will follow OAC 3701-60-06 on fees, reverification and the employment-service exception. This policy meets the following official items:

- OAC 3701-60-06(E) (Investigation fee): the agency pays BCI the prescribed fee for each criminal records check. The agency may charge the applicant a fee up to that amount only if it gives notice at the time of the initial application and Medicaid does not reimburse the fee.
- OAC 3701-60-06(H) (Reverification): the agency may request and accept reverification of a criminal records check that was completed within the previous twelve months.
- OAC 3701-60-06(I) (Employment-service exception): the agency need not request a check on an applicant referred by an employment service if the service confirms that it completed the database review and a criminal records check within one year, and both reports show no disqualifying offense.

The agency's default practice is that [AGENCY NAME] pays the BCI fee and does not charge applicants. Any change to that practice requires written approval of the Administrator and the notice described below. The database review in PER-04 is still the agency's responsibility in every case.

definitions.definition: The fee set by BCI for each criminal records check, paid by the agency to BCI.
The agency's request that BCI confirm the results of a criminal records check completed within the previous twelve months.
A business that refers applicants to the agency and has itself carried out the database review and criminal records check.

procedures: The designee pays the BCI fee for each check from agency funds when the request is made, and records the date, amount and check number or payment method in the Background Check Fee Log.

As a default, the agency does not charge applicants for the BCI fee. The agency may charge an applicant only if the Administrator approves in writing, the applicant receives written notice at the time of the initial application, and the Medicaid program does not reimburse the fee.

If a fee will be charged, the notice states the amount, which may not exceed the BCI fee the agency pays, and is signed by the applicant. The agency never deducts the fee without a signed notice, and never charges the applicant any amount that exceeds what it pays BCI.
The designee tells every applicant at application of any fingerprinting fee, as described in PER-05, and records that notice.
The designee does not charge a PCA a fee that would bring pay below the wage required by law. Any such deduction is reviewed under PER-14 before it is made.

If an applicant gives the agency a criminal records check completed within the previous twelve months, the designee asks the Administrator to approve a request for reverification in the manner BCI allows.

The designee confirms that the check is within twelve months of the date of the reverification request, records the original check date, and files the reverification response in the confidential background-check file.

A reverification will not be used if the check is more than twelve months old, if its source cannot be confirmed, or if the Administrator has any concern about the result. In those cases the agency requests a new check under PER-05.

If an applicant is referred by an employment service, the designee asks the service for written confirmation that (a) the database review and (b) a criminal records check were completed within one year, and that both reports show no disqualifying offense.

The designee reviews the written confirmation and files it. If the confirmation is incomplete, more than one year old, or shows any disqualifying offense, the agency does not use the exception and conducts its own database review and criminal records check.
Even when the exception applies, the designee still completes the agency's database review under PER-04 and records the hire date so that the five-year recheck in PER-06 is scheduled.
The Administrator reviews the Fee Log and all uses of reverification and the exception each quarter, and reports any exceptions to the governing body under GOV-05.

responsibilities.duty: Approves any applicant charge, approves reverification and use of the employment-service exception, and reviews quarterly.
Pays fees, gives fee notices, requests reverification, obtains the service's written confirmation and keeps records.
Provides written confirmation of the database review and the check, and the dates and results.

documentation: Background Check Fee Log (date, amount, payment method)
Signed fee notice, if an applicant is charged
Reverification request and BCI response, with the date of the original check
Employment service written confirmation
Agency database review printouts (PER-04)
Quarterly review record

policies.title: Conditional Employment and Disqualifying Offenses
policies.applies_to: All applicants and employees who would provide direct care to clients, the Administrator, the Compliance Officer, and anyone who makes or approves hiring decisions.
policies.purpose: To make sure no person who is barred from direct care by Ohio law works for [AGENCY NAME], and to set strict limits on when a caregiver may start work before the criminal records check is complete.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will not employ, or keep in a direct-care position, any applicant or employee who appears in the databases the state requires us to review or who has a disqualifying offense, except where the ODH rules allow an exception and the exception is documented under this policy (ORC 3740.11). The agency's default is that no one provides direct care until the criminal records check is complete and clear. Conditional employment is allowed only when all three conditions in OAC 3701-60-07 are met: (1) the database review is clear, (2) fingerprints are submitted before the person starts work, and (3) the BCI criminal records check is requested within 5 business days of the conditional hire. A conditional employee is terminated if the results are not received within 60 days or if the results show a disqualifying offense. Anyone who becomes disqualified after hire is removed from direct care immediately. This policy works together with PER-04 through PER-07. Criminal records reports are confidential.

definitions.definition: Starting an employee in direct care before the BCI criminal records check results are received, allowed only when all conditions of this policy are met.
Hands-on or in-person services to a client in the client's home, including personal care.
The review of the state and federal databases and registries that ORC 3740.11 requires before an applicant is employed, as listed in PER-04.

An offense listed in the ODH nonmedical home health criminal records check rules that bars a person from direct-care employment unless an ODH exception applies. The Compliance Officer keeps the current rule text on file and updates this reference when ODH amends the rule.
Any day Monday through Friday that is not a legal holiday.

procedures: Before any offer of direct-care work, the Compliance Officer completes and documents the database review described in PER-04. The review date and result are recorded on the Criminal Records Check Tracking Form.
If the database review shows a listed database hit, the applicant is not hired for direct care. The Compliance Officer records the result and notifies the Administrator the same day.

If the database review is clear, the default is to wait for the BCI result before the person starts direct care. Conditional employment may be used only if the Administrator approves it in writing and every condition in steps 4 to 6 is met.
Condition 1 - Clear database review: the Compliance Officer confirms the database review is complete, dated and clear before conditional status is granted.

Condition 2 - Fingerprints submitted before start: the applicant's fingerprints are taken and submitted to BCI under PER-05 before the first day of work. The Compliance Officer files the fingerprint receipt or transaction confirmation. No fingerprint confirmation means no start date.

Condition 3 - Check requested within 5 business days: the Compliance Officer submits the BCI request no later than 5 business days after the conditional hire date and records the request date. The Compliance Officer calendars the deadline when the conditional hire is approved.

The Compliance Officer opens a conditional employment record showing the hire date, database review date, fingerprint date, BCI request date and the 60-day deadline. To be safe, the 60-day deadline is counted from the first day of conditional employment unless the current ODH rule text says otherwise.

The Administrator gives the person a written notice that employment is conditional and that it ends if results are not received within 60 days or if they show a disqualifying offense. The employee signs the notice and a copy is filed in the personnel record.
The Compliance Officer checks the status of each pending BCI result at least weekly. Results are reviewed only by the Compliance Officer and the Administrator.

When results are received, the Compliance Officer reviews them against the current list of disqualifying offenses within 1 business day and records the outcome. If the results are clear, the employee's status changes to regular employment and the conditional record is closed.

If the results show a disqualifying offense, the Administrator removes the person from all direct care the same day and terminates employment. The Administrator reviews whether any ODH exception applies before making a final decision. The agency employs the person only if the exception criteria in the current ODH rule are fully met and the Administrator documents the basis in writing.

If results have not been received by the 60-day deadline, the Administrator terminates the conditional employment on or before that date. The agency may reapply the person only by starting a new check under PER-05.

For all current employees, the Compliance Officer uses the recheck process in PER-06 to identify anyone who has become disqualified. Each caregiver must tell the Administrator within 1 business day of any arrest, charge, indictment or conviction, or any listing in a database.

When an employee becomes disqualified or is reported to be disqualified, the Administrator removes the employee from direct care immediately, pending verification. If the disqualification is confirmed, employment ends.
The Administrator informs the case management agency or payer only as required by program rules (see SVC-12) and arranges replacement coverage under SVC-08 so clients are not left without services.
Criminal records reports and results are kept in a locked, access-restricted file separate from the general personnel file. They are not disclosed except as the law allows (see CR-03 and PER-13).
The Compliance Officer reviews the conditional employment tracker monthly and reports to the Administrator any conditional hire that is within 14 days of its deadline.

responsibilities.duty: Approves each conditional hire in writing, removes disqualified staff from direct care, makes final decisions on exceptions, and terminates employment when required.
Completes the database review, submits fingerprints and BCI requests, tracks the 5-business-day and 60-day deadlines, reviews results, and keeps the current disqualifying offense rule text on file.
Submits fingerprints before starting, signs the conditional employment notice, and reports arrests, charges and convictions within 1 business day.

documentation: Criminal Records Check Tracking Form with database review date and result
Fingerprint submission confirmation filed before the start date
BCI request confirmation showing the request date
Conditional employment notice signed by the employee
Administrator's written approval of conditional hire
Documentation of results review and the outcome
Termination or removal record and any written exception decision
Monthly conditional employment tracker

policies.title: Orientation of Caregivers
policies.applies_to: All newly hired personal care aides (PCAs) and any other caregiver who will have in-person client contact, and the staff who deliver orientation.
policies.purpose: To make sure every caregiver understands the agency's expectations, ethical standards, communication lines, reporting duties and safety practices before meeting any client in person.
policies.policy: This policy meets OAC 173-39-02.11(C)(3)(b)(i)-(vii) (item C(3)(b) - Orientation before direct in-person contact). Every caregiver completes [AGENCY NAME]'s orientation before any direct in-person contact with a client. Orientation covers all seven required topics: (i) the provider's expectations of employees, (ii) ethical standards under OAC 173-39-02, (iii) an overview of personnel policies, (iv) the organization and lines of communication of the agency, (v) incident-reporting procedures, (vi) emergency procedures, and (vii) standard precautions for infection control. A signed orientation checklist is kept for every caregiver. Orientation hours do not count toward the 6 hours of annual in-service training (see PER-11).

definitions.definition: The agency's required introductory training given before a caregiver's first in-person client contact.
Any face-to-face contact with a client, including shadowing visits and introductions at the client's home.
Infection control practices applied to all clients, including hand hygiene, glove use and safe handling of soiled items.

procedures: The Administrator or designee schedules orientation as soon as a caregiver accepts an offer. The caregiver's first client assignment date is set after the orientation completion date.
The Compliance Officer confirms that the hiring steps in PER-01, PER-02 and PER-04 through PER-08 are complete before the caregiver is scheduled for any client contact.
The trainer gives the caregiver the orientation packet: the agency's policy summaries, code of conduct, organization chart, communication contacts and incident forms.
Topic (i) - Expectations of employees: the trainer reviews attendance, punctuality, dress, EVV use, documentation, care plan adherence and the job description (PER-03).

Topic (ii) - Ethical standards under OAC 173-39-02: the trainer reviews professional boundaries, client rights, prohibited gifts and loans, confidentiality and exploitation prevention (CR-01, CR-03, CR-04, PER-15).
Topic (iii) - Overview of personnel policies: the trainer covers hours, pay practices, training requirements, health policy, discipline and how to raise concerns (PER-09 to PER-15).

Topic (iv) - Organization and lines of communication: the trainer shows the organization chart and explains who the caregiver reports to, how to reach the supervisor and the Administrator at [PHONE], and how to reach someone after hours.

Topic (v) - Incident-reporting procedures: the trainer explains what must be reported, the time limits in SAF-02, how to report abuse, neglect or exploitation under SAF-01, and how to complete the incident form.
Topic (vi) - Emergency procedures: the trainer reviews when to call 911, steps for a fall, injury or sudden illness, fire and severe weather, and who to notify afterward (SVC-10, SAF-05).
Topic (vii) - Standard precautions for infection control: the trainer teaches and demonstrates hand hygiene, glove use and disposal, and cleaning of surfaces and equipment (SAF-03, SAF-04).
The trainer checks understanding with a short question session or return demonstration for hand hygiene and gloving, and records any follow-up needed.
The caregiver and trainer sign and date the Orientation Checklist, which lists each of the seven topics, the date and the hours spent.
The Administrator or Compliance Officer reviews the checklist and releases the caregiver for client contact only when every topic is checked and the checklist is signed.
The checklist is filed in the personnel record. The orientation hours are not added to the in-service log (PER-11).
If a caregiver misses part of orientation, the missed topic is completed and signed off before any client contact. No partial release is allowed.
When a policy covered in orientation changes materially, the trainer updates the orientation content and notes the revision date (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure orientation is delivered and that no caregiver has client contact before completing it.
Delivers all seven topics, checks understanding and signs the orientation checklist.
Audits orientation checklists against start dates and client assignments each month.
Attends all orientation, asks questions and signs the checklist.

documentation: Signed Orientation Checklist listing all seven topics (i)-(vii), with date and hours
Orientation packet receipt
Record of any makeup session
Monthly audit comparing orientation completion dates to first client contact dates

policies.title: Competency Evaluation and Additional Training
policies.applies_to: All PCAs and caregivers, supervisors who assign tasks, and the staff who train or evaluate caregivers.
policies.purpose: To make sure that no caregiver performs a task for which the caregiver has not been trained and shown to be competent.
policies.policy: This policy meets OAC 173-39-02.11(C)(3)(c) (item C(3)(c) - Additional training and competency evaluation if the PCA will perform activities for which the PCA was not trained or evaluated). If a PCA will perform an activity that the PCA has not previously been trained on or evaluated for, [AGENCY NAME] provides additional training and a competency evaluation first. The task is not assigned until the PCA passes the evaluation and the result is documented. Initial qualifications of each PCA are verified under PER-01 and PER-02 (OAC 173-39-02.11(C)(3)(a)).

definitions.definition: A documented check, using direct observation or return demonstration, that a caregiver can perform a task safely and correctly.
Instruction given for a task not covered in the caregiver's initial training or prior evaluation.
An activity listed in the client's service plan that the caregiver is assigned to perform.

procedures: At intake and each service plan update, the Supervisor compares each task in the client's service plan with the assigned caregiver's training and competency records (SVC-03).
The Supervisor checks that each task is within the agency's allowed scope of services (SVC-01). Tasks outside scope are not assigned and are referred under SVC-01 and SVC-12.
If the caregiver's file does not show training and an evaluation for the task, the Supervisor flags it as a competency gap before the first visit.
The Supervisor does not assign the task to that caregiver, and arranges another caregiver who is already competent, until the gap is closed.

The Supervisor selects the training method (classroom, demonstration or supervised practice) and schedules it. Training on a new task is delivered by a person qualified in the task, as set out in SVC-05.
After training, a qualified evaluator observes the caregiver perform the task and rates each step on the Competency Evaluation Form as pass or not yet competent.
If the caregiver does not pass, the evaluator gives specific feedback, arranges further practice and re-evaluates. The task stays unassigned until a pass is recorded.
The evaluator and the caregiver sign and date the form. The Supervisor confirms the pass and clears the task for assignment on the same day.
The completed form is filed in the personnel record within 5 business days and the competency list in the scheduling system is updated.

Where client-specific instruction is needed (for example, how a client uses a particular transfer aid), the Supervisor demonstrates and documents it on the client's service plan and in the caregiver's record.
Caregivers must tell the Supervisor before the visit if they are asked to do any task they have not been trained on. They must not perform it. The Supervisor records the report.

If a caregiver is found to have performed an unevaluated task, the Supervisor stops the practice, records it as an incident under SAF-02, checks for client harm and completes training and evaluation before the task is assigned again.

Competency re-checks are done when a caregiver's performance raises a concern, after a change in the client's condition that changes how a task is done, or when the Supervisor notes a skill problem during a supervisory visit (SVC-04).

The Compliance Officer audits a sample of service plans and personnel files each quarter to confirm that every assigned task has a matching competency record and reports the results to the QA committee (GOV-05).
Time spent in additional training and evaluation is paid working time (PER-14). It does not count toward the 6 hours of annual in-service unless the training meets in-service requirements (PER-11).

responsibilities.duty: Identifies gaps, withholds assignment, arranges training and evaluation, and clears the task for assignment.
Observes the caregiver, records results on the Competency Evaluation Form and signs it.
Audits task assignments against competency records.
Performs only tasks for which trained and evaluated, and reports any request to do otherwise.

documentation: Competency Evaluation Form signed by evaluator and caregiver
Training attendance record for additional training
Competency gap flag and resolution record
Updated caregiver competency list
Quarterly audit results

policies.title: Annual In-Service Training
policies.applies_to: All PCAs and caregivers employed by [AGENCY NAME], the training coordinator, and the Administrator.
policies.purpose: To keep caregivers' skills current through annual training that meets Ohio program requirements.
policies.policy: This policy meets OAC 173-39-02.11(C)(3)(d) (item C(3)(d) - In-service training: each PCA completes six hours of ODA-approved in-service training every twelve months under ORC 173.525; agency- and program-specific orientation do not count toward the six hours). Each PCA completes at least 6 hours of ODA-approved in-service training every 12 months. Orientation does not count toward the 6 hours. The same 6-hour requirement applies to personal care under the Older Americans Act (OAC 173-3-06.5). Agency aides serving Ohio Home Care Waiver clients complete 8 in-service hours a year under OAC 5160-46-04, and the agency applies the higher requirement to any aide who serves those clients. Training hours are tracked in a log, and training time is paid as the wage-hour law requires (PER-14).

definitions.definition: Continuing education for current caregivers, in topics approved by ODA, apart from orientation.
Training that meets ODA's requirements for approved in-service content and providers. The Compliance Officer confirms approval before counting any course.
The twelve months beginning on the caregiver's date of hire and each anniversary of it, unless the agency documents a different consistent cycle.

procedures: The Administrator designates a training coordinator, who maintains the annual training plan and the In-Service Training Log for every caregiver.
At hire, the coordinator enters the caregiver's date of hire and the end of the first 12-month period in the log.
The coordinator flags in the log any caregiver who serves Ohio Home Care Waiver clients as requiring 8 hours, and all other PCAs as requiring 6 hours.

The coordinator builds a yearly training calendar using topics relevant to the agency's clients, such as personal care skills, safe transfers, dementia care, infection control and abuse and neglect, and offers sessions so every caregiver can finish well before the deadline.
Before counting a course, the coordinator confirms that it is ODA-approved and records the provider, topic, date and hours. Courses that cannot be confirmed as approved are not counted.

Orientation hours (PER-09) and agency-specific training on new tasks (PER-10) are recorded separately and are not counted toward the 6 hours unless the course independently meets ODA's in-service approval.
The caregiver receives and gives the coordinator a certificate or attendance record for each course within 5 business days. The coordinator files it and updates the log.

The coordinator runs a report on the 1st of each month listing each caregiver's hours completed and hours remaining, and sends reminders to caregivers with fewer than the required hours and 90 days or less left in the period.
At 30 days before a caregiver's period ends, the coordinator notifies the Supervisor and the Administrator of any caregiver who is short of the requirement and schedules makeup training.
A caregiver who has not completed the required hours by the end of the 12-month period is not scheduled for client visits until the hours are completed, and the Administrator documents this decision.

Training time is paid working time and counted for overtime as required by wage-hour law. If training takes place away from the usual worksite, the Administrator applies PER-14 for travel time. Training is not a deduction from pay and is not charged to the caregiver.
The coordinator verifies and files supporting records, including certificates, in the personnel file in accordance with PER-13 and keeps them for the employment period plus 6 years (OAC 173-39-02).
The Compliance Officer audits the In-Service Training Log each quarter against certificates and reports to the QA committee (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the training plan and budget, and decides on removal from scheduling when hours are not completed.
Maintains the log, confirms ODA approval of courses, sends reminders and files certificates.
Schedules caregivers around training and identifies training needs from supervisory visits.
Completes at least the required hours each 12-month period and provides certificates.

documentation: In-Service Training Log for each caregiver
Certificates or attendance records for each course
Annual training calendar
Monthly hours-remaining report
Quarterly audit results
Payroll records showing paid training time

policies.title: Employee Health and TB Screening
policies.applies_to: All employees and volunteers who have contact with clients, and the Administrator and Compliance Officer.
policies.purpose: To protect clients and staff from the spread of communicable disease and to protect the privacy of employee health information.
policies.policy: The Ohio rules reviewed for this manual do not set a specific tuberculosis (TB) screening requirement for nonmedical home health agencies. [AGENCY NAME] therefore adopts its own employee health screening policy as set out below and will confirm any additional requirement with the Ohio Department of Health (ODH) and with the Medicaid programs it serves. If a program or ODH requires something more, the Administrator updates this policy under GOV-04. Employees with a communicable illness are excluded from client contact. Employees whose duties could expose them to blood or other potentially infectious materials are covered by OSHA's bloodborne pathogens standard (29 CFR 1910.1030) and SAF-04. Health records are kept in a file separate from personnel records.

definitions.definition: An illness that can spread from one person to another, such as influenza, COVID-19, active TB, infectious diarrhea, or a contagious rash.
A health questionnaire and any tests or review the agency requires before client contact, completed as set out in this policy.
Records of screening, test results, vaccinations, declinations and work restrictions, kept confidentially and apart from the personnel file.

procedures: Before the first client contact, each new caregiver completes the agency's Employee Health Screening Form, which asks about symptoms of communicable disease and exposure history.

As agency policy, each new caregiver also provides a TB screening result (symptom screen and a TB test or evidence of a prior documented result) before client contact. The Administrator confirms with ODH whether any further requirement applies and records the confirmation.
If a screening result is positive or shows symptoms, the caregiver is not scheduled for client contact until a health care provider's written clearance is received.
The agency pays for the screening it requires, or reimburses the employee, and does not require employees to bear the cost of tests the agency mandates.

For employees with a reasonably anticipated risk of exposure to blood or other potentially infectious materials, the agency offers hepatitis B vaccination at no cost within the time set by 29 CFR 1910.1030, and documents any declination. These steps are detailed in SAF-04.

The agency encourages, but does not require unless otherwise directed by a payer or by law, annual influenza and other recommended vaccinations, and records any health-related decisions in the health file.

Each employee must report to the Supervisor, before the scheduled start of a shift, any symptoms such as fever, vomiting, diarrhea, a new cough or a draining skin lesion, and must not report to a client's home while ill.
When an employee reports symptoms, the Supervisor arranges replacement coverage under SVC-07 and SVC-08 and tells the caregiver when the exclusion ends.

As general guidance, an employee returns to client contact when symptoms have resolved and, for illnesses with an established exclusion period, when that period has passed or a health care provider's written release is provided.

The Administrator reports an exposure of a client to a communicable illness through staff to the client's physician or case manager where appropriate, and records the event as an incident under SAF-02.
Employee health information is shared only with those who need it to carry out this policy. It is not disclosed to clients or co-workers.
Health records are kept in a locked file or access-controlled system, separate from the personnel file and from criminal records (PER-13), and are retained as required by law and by PER-13.
The Administrator reviews this policy at least annually and after any public health directive, and updates it under GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Sets and updates the health screening requirements, confirms rules with ODH, and approves return to work.
Receives illness reports, excludes ill employees from client contact and arranges coverage.
Keeps health records separate and confidential and audits for screening completion.
Completes screening, reports symptoms before a shift and stays out of client homes while ill.

documentation: Employee Health Screening Form
TB screening result or clearance letter
Hepatitis B vaccination or declination form (see SAF-04)
Work exclusion and return-to-work notes
Written confirmation from ODH or payer on any further requirement
Separate, confidential employee health file

policies.title: Personnel Records
policies.applies_to: All current and former employees, applicants, the Administrator, the Compliance Officer and anyone with access to personnel files.
policies.purpose: To make sure personnel records are complete, secure, kept for the required period and available to state and federal agencies on demand.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a personnel file for every employee. Qualification records are kept for the period of employment plus 6 years (OAC 173-39-02(B)). Training certificates, the nurse aide registry printout and proof of prior employment are kept as required by OAC 173-39-02.11(C)(3). ODA, ODM, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the Auditor of State are given immediate access to records on request. Criminal records check reports are confidential under ORC 3740.11 and are kept in a separate, restricted file. Health records are kept apart from personnel files (PER-12).

definitions.definition: The record of an employee's application, qualifications, training, evaluations, job description and conduct acknowledgments.
Documents proving a caregiver meets the rules to work as a caregiver, including certificates, registry printouts and prior-employment proof.
Producing requested records to an authorized agency representative at the time of the request, without delay for review or approval.

procedures: The Administrator opens a personnel file for each applicant who receives a conditional or final offer, and the Compliance Officer maintains it.

Each file contains: application and résumé; screening results summary; proof of qualifications (training certificate or competency documentation, nurse aide registry printout, and proof of prior employment where relied on); signed orientation checklist (PER-09); competency evaluations (PER-10); in-service log and certificates (PER-11); signed job description (PER-03); and the signed conduct and professional boundaries acknowledgment (PER-15).

Documents reflecting the BCI criminal records check and database results are not filed in the general file. The general file holds only a verification sheet stating the date the check was done, that the person was cleared, and the next recheck date.

Criminal records reports are kept confidential under ORC 3740.11. They are stored in a locked cabinet or access-controlled electronic folder that only the Administrator and Compliance Officer may open.
Health records, such as TB results and vaccination or declination forms, are stored in a separate locked file under PER-12 and are not placed in the personnel file.
Wage, hour and payroll records are kept as set out in PER-14 and may be cross-referenced in the file.
The Compliance Officer completes the Personnel File Checklist at hire and confirms that every required item is present before the caregiver has client contact.
The Compliance Officer audits all files at least annually, plus 10 percent monthly, and corrects any missing or expired items. Findings go to the Administrator and the QA committee (GOV-05).
Employees may review their own personnel files on request with notice and with the Compliance Officer present, but may not remove documents.

Access to personnel files is limited to the Administrator, Compliance Officer, Supervisors who need the information and authorized government representatives. Staff sign an access log when they open a file.

When ODA, ODM, HHS or the Auditor of State asks for records, the Administrator or Compliance Officer provides them immediately and records the request, who made it and what was provided. If neither is on site, the senior staff member present provides access and contacts the Administrator at [PHONE] right away (REC-03).
Electronic records are backed up daily and protected by password, access controls and an audit trail. Paper records are kept at the business site at [ADDRESS] in locked storage (REC-03).

Qualification records are kept for the full period of employment plus 6 years. Service records, which are not part of the personnel file, are kept for 6 years after payment or until any review or audit ends, whichever is later (REC-01).
Records are not destroyed while an audit, review, investigation or legal action is pending. The Administrator places a hold on any affected records.
At the end of the retention period, the Compliance Officer approves destruction by shredding or secure electronic deletion and keeps a destruction log.
When an employee leaves, the Compliance Officer closes the file, records the separation date and sets the destruction date as 6 years after the end of employment.

responsibilities.duty: Is responsible for the integrity of personnel records, approves destruction and makes sure government access requests are met immediately.
Maintains files, keeps criminal records and health records separate, runs audits and keeps the retention schedule.
Provides training, evaluation and supervisory documents for the file and respects access limits.
Provides accurate documents, updates contact information and certificates, and keeps file information confidential.

documentation: Personnel File Checklist
Criminal records check verification sheet (general file) and restricted criminal records file
File access log
Record request log for government agency access
Annual and monthly file audit results
Retention schedule and destruction log
Records hold notices

policies.title: Wage, Hour and Overtime Compliance
policies.applies_to: Administrator, payroll and scheduling staff, and all hourly caregivers and PCA Supervisors
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] pays every employee lawfully for all time worked, meets Ohio and federal wage and hour requirements, and can truthfully make the wage-hour and workers' compensation attestations required of ODA-certified agency providers.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] pays every non-exempt employee at least the applicable minimum wage for all hours worked. The 2026 Ohio minimum wage is $11.00 per hour for non-tipped employees. It applies to employers above $405,000 in gross receipts; smaller employers stay at the federal minimum wage under the FLSA. The agency determines each year which standard applies and pays at the higher of the applicable state or federal rate. As a third-party employer of home care workers, the agency follows the FLSA and 29 CFR 552 and does not treat caregivers as exempt from minimum wage or overtime. Time worked includes time with the client, required training and orientation, required meetings, and travel time between clients during the workday. Hours over 40 in a workweek are paid at one and one-half times the regular rate. The agency displays the official 2026 Ohio minimum wage poster. The agency registers with the Ohio Bureau of Workers' Compensation (BWC) and the Ohio Department of Job and Family Services (ODJFS) before its first payroll. As an ODA-certified agency provider, it attests to compliance with wage-hour and workers' compensation requirements and with tax payment (OAC 173-39-02(C)(1)).

definitions.definition: A fixed, recurring period of 168 hours (seven consecutive 24-hour days) set by the agency and used for all overtime calculations.
All time an employee is required or permitted to work, including client visits, paid travel between clients, training, orientation and required meetings.
The employee's hourly pay plus other required earnings in the workweek, used to calculate overtime.
An employee entitled to minimum wage and overtime. All caregivers are non-exempt.

procedures: Before the first payroll, the Administrator registers [AGENCY NAME] with Ohio BWC for workers' compensation coverage and with ODJFS for unemployment compensation, and files the confirmations in the corporate compliance file.

Before hiring, the Administrator confirms the applicable minimum wage for the agency. Each January the Administrator reviews the Ohio Department of Commerce notice and records whether gross receipts exceed $405,000. This sets whether the $11.00 Ohio rate or the federal minimum wage applies.
The Administrator sets every caregiver's starting wage at no less than the applicable minimum wage and documents the rate in the personnel file and on the offer letter.

The Administrator posts the official 2026 Ohio minimum wage poster at the business site [ADDRESS] where employees can read it. The poster is replaced each year when the Department of Commerce issues a new one.
The Administrator defines the agency's fixed workweek in writing and applies it to every payroll period.

Caregivers record actual start and end times for every visit through the Electronic Visit Verification system (see SVC-09). Time spent on other paid activities is recorded on a timesheet approved by the supervisor.
Payroll staff treat time between consecutive clients on the same workday as paid time. Payroll staff compare visit times against the schedule so that travel time is not left out.
Payroll treats orientation, competency evaluation and annual in-service training (PER-09, PER-10, PER-11) as paid hours worked.

Employees do not perform off-the-clock work. Supervisors may not tell employees to work before clocking in or after clocking out. An employee who works unscheduled time reports it, and the time is paid.

The Scheduler reviews weekly hours every day for each caregiver. When a caregiver is projected to exceed 40 hours, the Scheduler tells the Administrator before the schedule is changed so that overtime is approved in advance. Approval may not be used to avoid paying time actually worked.
Payroll pays all hours over 40 in the workweek at one and one-half times the regular rate. Payroll computes the regular rate to include other required earnings.
Payroll issues each employee a pay statement every pay period showing hours worked, rate, overtime hours and deductions.
Payroll compares the lowest paid rate against the applicable minimum wage at each pay run and corrects any shortfall in the next payroll. The Administrator documents the correction.

The Administrator reviews the agency's compliance with wage-hour, workers' compensation and tax obligations each quarter. Each year, before signing any ODA attestation, the Administrator confirms that the attestation is accurate.
The Administrator retains payroll, time and wage records as set in PER-13 and REC-01.

Employees who believe they were paid incorrectly report the concern to the Administrator. The Administrator investigates within 10 business days, corrects any underpayment, and does not retaliate against the employee.

responsibilities.duty: Registers with BWC and ODJFS, verifies the applicable minimum wage each year, posts the poster, approves overtime, signs attestations and reviews compliance quarterly.
Calculate hours worked including travel time and training, pay overtime, issue pay statements and keep payroll records.
Monitors weekly hours and notifies the Administrator before a caregiver is projected to exceed 40 hours.
Record all time worked accurately and report any pay errors.

documentation: BWC and ODJFS registration confirmations
Annual minimum wage determination record
Posted 2026 poster verification
EVV and timesheet records
Payroll registers and pay statements
Overtime approval records
Quarterly wage-hour compliance review
ODA attestations on file

policies.title: Staff Conduct and Professional Boundaries
policies.applies_to: All employees, caregivers, PCA Supervisors, volunteers and contractors of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To set ethical, professional, respectful and legal standards of conduct for everyone who serves clients, to protect clients from harm and exploitation, and to meet the ODA and ODM conduct requirements for provider certification and participation.
policies.policy: This policy meets OAC 173-39-02(B)(8)(a)-(n) (Ethical, professional, respectful and legal service standards, item B(8)) and OAC 173-39-02(C)(1)(c) (written policies requiring employees to provide services in a manner compliant with (B)(8), item C(1)(c)). [AGENCY NAME] does not allow unethical, unprofessional, disrespectful or illegal behavior. Every employee must provide services in a manner that complies with paragraph (B)(8) of OAC 173-39-02. Under this policy and the rule, staff may not: (1) use or be under the influence of alcohol while providing services; (2) use or be under the influence of illegal or non-prescribed drugs, or be impaired, while providing services; (3) accept gifts or tips from a client or the client's family; (4) engage in sexual conduct with a client; (5) leave the client's home during service except as the service plan authorizes; (6) fail to cooperate with ODA, ODM or the case management agency; (7) engage in distracting activities, including personal calls, texting or social media use, that take attention from the client; (8) abuse a client or cause the client distress, including posting or sharing a client's photo or information on social media without the client's written consent; (9) form a personal relationship with a client beyond the professional relationship; (10) take on a decision-making role for a client; (11) sell items or services to a client or buy from a client; (12) use the client's food or property for the employee's own purposes; (13) take a client to the agency's business site; and (14) engage in any conflict of interest. For Ohio Home Care Waiver and other ODM-funded services (OAC 5160-44-31), staff also may not sleep while on duty, bring visitors to the client's home, work while impaired, give or take gifts or loans, falsify signatures, or act as the client's power of attorney or guardian. Staff sign this policy at hire and every year. Violations lead to discipline up to and including termination and may be reported to authorities.

definitions.definition: A situation where an employee's personal, financial or other interest could influence, or appear to influence, the employee's judgment in serving a client.
The limit between a caregiver's role and a client's personal life, which protects the client from exploitation or confusion about the relationship.
Any activity that diverts a caregiver's attention from the client, such as personal phone use, television, visitors or personal errands.
Acting as a client's power of attorney, guardian, agent, payee or other legal or financial decision-maker, or making personal, medical or financial decisions for the client.

procedures: The Administrator keeps the written Staff Conduct Standards, which restate each prohibition in the Policy section in plain language, as part of this policy. The Standards are reviewed annually under GOV-04.
During hiring, the Administrator or designee explains the Standards to every applicant before the offer is accepted.
On the first day of employment and before any client contact, each employee reads and signs the Staff Conduct Standards acknowledgment. The signed copy goes in the personnel file (PER-13).
Each year, within 30 days of the employee's anniversary date, the PCA Supervisor reviews the Standards with the employee. The employee signs again and the new acknowledgment is filed.
Orientation (PER-09) includes a conduct session using examples such as tips offered by clients, requests to borrow money, requests to run personal errands, and invitations to social media.

Caregivers decline gifts and tips politely by explaining that agency policy does not allow them. They report any offer or attempt to give a gift, tip or loan to the PCA Supervisor within one business day so the agency can document it and, if needed, talk with the client or family.
Caregivers do not use cell phones for personal purposes during client visits. They may use a phone for emergencies, for contacting the agency, and for EVV where the system requires it (SVC-09).

Caregivers do not take photographs or video of clients or their homes, and do not post anything about a client on social media. Photos for any agency purpose require the client's written consent, kept in the client record.

If a caregiver must leave the home during a visit, the caregiver does so only when the service plan authorizes it (for example, a planned errand) or in an emergency. The caregiver notes the time and reason in the visit record.

A caregiver who has a personal or financial relationship with a client, or who is asked to take a decision-making role, tells the Administrator immediately. The Administrator decides within 2 business days whether the caregiver may continue to serve the client and documents the decision.
Caregivers do not use a client's food, supplies, vehicle or other property for their own use. They do not sell products or services to clients or buy from clients.

A caregiver who suspects alcohol or drug use or impairment in a coworker reports it to the Administrator immediately. The Administrator removes the person from client contact the same day pending review.
Any staff member who sees or suspects a violation reports it to the Administrator within one business day. The Administrator documents the report and begins an investigation within 2 business days.
If the violation involves abuse, neglect or exploitation, the Administrator follows SAF-01 and reports to Adult Protective Services and to ODA or its designee within one business day as required.

If the investigation confirms a violation, the Administrator applies discipline consistently, up to termination, and documents the action in the personnel file. The Administrator reports to regulators or law enforcement where required.
Staff cooperate fully and promptly with ODA, ODM, the case management agency and ODH in any review, audit or investigation.
The Administrator reviews conduct complaints and confirmed violations each quarter as part of quality assurance (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the Standards, ensures every employee signs at hire and yearly, investigates violations and applies discipline.
Reviews the Standards with employees, monitors conduct during supervisory visits and reports concerns.
Comply with every standard, report offers of gifts and any violation, and cooperate with investigations.

documentation: Signed Staff Conduct Standards acknowledgments at hire and yearly
Orientation sign-in and conduct session record
Gift or tip offer reports
Conflict of interest determinations
Investigation and discipline records
Client social media consent forms, if any

policies.title: Supervision of Volunteers
policies.applies_to: Administrator, PCA Supervisors and any volunteers used by [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure any volunteers who assist [AGENCY NAME] are supervised, protect clients, and keep client information confidential.
policies.policy: This policy meets OAC 173-39-02(B)(6) (The provider shall supervise the provider's volunteers, item B(6)). [AGENCY NAME] supervises every volunteer it uses. A volunteer works only under the direction of a named supervisor. Volunteers do not provide hands-on personal care unless they meet the qualifications for the task set in PER-01 and are approved by the Administrator. Volunteers are not scheduled in place of paid caregivers for services billed to a payer, and the agency does not bill any payer for volunteer time. Every volunteer signs a confidentiality agreement and the Staff Conduct Standards (PER-15) before beginning. Volunteers are screened as set in PER-04 before any client contact.

definitions.definition: A person who provides unpaid services or assistance on behalf of [AGENCY NAME] and is not a paid employee.
Direct physical assistance with activities such as bathing, toileting, dressing and transferring.

procedures: The Administrator decides whether the agency will use volunteers and defines the volunteer roles in writing (for example, friendly visiting or office help). Roles do not include hands-on personal care unless the volunteer is qualified under PER-01.
The Administrator assigns each volunteer to a named supervisor, who is a PCA Supervisor or the Administrator.
Before any client contact, the Administrator screens each volunteer as set in PER-04, including the database and criminal records review applicable under that policy, and records the result.
A volunteer who has a disqualifying result under PER-04 and PER-08 does not work with clients.
Each volunteer signs a confidentiality agreement and the Staff Conduct Standards acknowledgment (PER-15) before beginning. The signed copies are filed in the volunteer file.

The supervisor gives each volunteer a documented orientation covering client rights (CR-01), privacy (CR-03), abuse and neglect reporting (SAF-01), emergencies (SAF-10 is not used; see SVC-10) and the limits of the volunteer's role. The supervisor records the date and content of the orientation.
The supervisor gives the volunteer written assignments that name the client or task, the date and time, and the tasks the volunteer may and may not do.
The supervisor checks the volunteer's work by direct observation or contact at least once during each new assignment, and afterward as often as needed. The supervisor documents each check.
Volunteers report any concern about a client, any incident, and any suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation to the supervisor immediately. The supervisor follows SAF-01 and SAF-02.

Volunteers may not accept gifts or money, drive clients, handle client money, give medication, or perform tasks outside the written role. A volunteer who is asked to do so declines and tells the supervisor.
The supervisor ends a volunteer's service and documents the reason if the volunteer violates this policy, the Standards or client confidentiality.
The Administrator keeps a current volunteer roster showing role, supervisor, screening date and agreement dates, and reviews it each year.

responsibilities.duty: Approves volunteer roles, completes screening, approves any exception, and keeps the roster.
Orients, assigns, observes and documents volunteer work, and removes a volunteer when needed.
Stay within the written role, keep information confidential, follow the conduct standards and report concerns immediately.

documentation: Written volunteer role descriptions
Volunteer screening records
Signed confidentiality and conduct agreements
Orientation records
Assignment sheets and supervision notes
Volunteer roster

policies.title: Client Records and Retention
policies.applies_to: Administrator, PCA Supervisors, office staff and caregivers who create or handle client records
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] creates complete, accurate, confidential client records, and keeps them for the legally required period so that services and billing can be verified by regulators and payers.
policies.policy: This policy meets OAC 173-39-02(B)(10)(a) (Records retention, item B(10)(a)). [AGENCY NAME] keeps service records for six years after payment, and until all reviews and audits are resolved if those last longer. [AGENCY NAME] keeps qualification records for the duration of certification or employment plus six years. For Ohio Home Care Waiver clients, the agency keeps a confidential clinical record at the place of business containing identifying data, the person-centered services plan (PCSP), allergies and dietary restrictions, advance directives, a task log with times and dated signatures, signed progress notes, and a discharge summary. For every visit, the record shows the tasks done or not done, the date, the location, start and end times, and the signatures of the provider and the client. If the client's signature was not obtained at the visit, it is obtained within 3 business days. Service and billing records for ODM waiver services are kept 6 years from payment or until any audit ends. Records are confidential (CR-03) and stored securely (REC-03). Records are never destroyed while an audit, review, investigation or legal action is open.

definitions.definition: Records showing services were authorized, delivered and billed, including the service plan, visit documentation, EVV data, claims and payment records.
Records showing a caregiver or supervisor met required qualifications, such as certification, background checks, training and competency evaluations.
The confidential Ohio Home Care Waiver client record kept at the place of business.
A written instruction to keep records beyond the normal retention period because of an audit, review, investigation or legal matter.

procedures: At admission, the PCA Supervisor opens a client record and files the identifying data, referral and eligibility documents, assessment, signed service agreement (CR-06) and the client's rights acknowledgment (CR-01).

For Ohio Home Care Waiver clients, the PCA Supervisor places the PCSP in the clinical record and records allergies, dietary restrictions and advance directive information. The supervisor updates these entries whenever the client's status changes.

The record contains the current service plan (SVC-03), task log, supervisory visit notes (SVC-04), incident reports (SAF-02), grievances (CR-02) and correspondence with the case management agency or payer.
At every visit, the caregiver documents the tasks done and not done, the date, the location, and the start and end times. EVV data supports these entries (SVC-09).

The caregiver obtains the client's signature and signs the visit record at the visit. If the client's signature could not be obtained at the visit, the caregiver or office staff obtains it within 3 business days, and the reason for the delay is noted.
The caregiver writes signed, dated progress notes that describe observations and any change in condition. The caregiver reports any change to the PCA Supervisor the same day (SVC-10).

Office staff check visit records weekly for completeness and signatures and return incomplete records to the caregiver for correction. Corrections are made by a single-line strike-through, initials and date, and never by erasing or backdating.
The agency does not bill a payer until the visit record and EVV data support the claim. Billing records are filed by client and month.
When service ends, the PCA Supervisor completes a discharge summary within 10 business days of the last date of service (SVC-11) and places it in the record.

After discharge, the Administrator closes the record, marks the date of the last payment received for the client, and calculates the destruction-eligible date as six years after that date, or later if an audit or review is open.
Personnel qualification records are kept in each personnel file (PER-13). The Administrator keeps them for the full length of employment and for six years after employment ends.
The Administrator keeps a retention log listing each record set, its retention trigger date and its earliest destruction date. The Administrator checks the log every year.

Before any destruction, the Administrator confirms that no audit, review, investigation or legal matter is open. If one is open, the Administrator places a hold in writing and keeps the records until it is released.

Paper records are destroyed by cross-cut shredding or a certified shredding vendor, and electronic records by secure deletion. The Administrator signs a destruction record listing what was destroyed and the date.
Records required for HIPAA policies and procedures, and for disclosures and acknowledgments, are kept for at least six years as 45 CFR 164.530 requires (see CR-03).
If the agency closes, the Administrator keeps all records for the required period, and tells ODA, ODM and ODH in writing where the records are stored and who is the custodian.

responsibilities.duty: Owns this policy, maintains the retention log, authorizes destruction and holds, and ensures records are available to regulators.
Opens and maintains client records, completes plans, notes and discharge summaries, and reviews visit documentation.
Complete accurate, timely visit documentation and obtain client signatures.
Check records for completeness, file records and support billing.

documentation: Client records (identifying data, PCSP, service plan, allergies and dietary restrictions, advance directives, task log, progress notes, discharge summary)
Visit records and EVV data
Billing and payment records
Retention log
Records hold notices
Destruction records

policies.title: Required Reports to the State
policies.applies_to: Administrator, PCA Supervisors and office staff responsible for notices and reports
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] sends every report and notice required by ODH, ODA and ODM on time, and can prove it did.
policies.policy: This policy meets OAC 173-39-02(B)(3)(c) (Notify ODA or its designee of any change in telephone number, mailing address or email address within seven days, item B(3)(c)) and addresses OAC 3701-60-06(I) (Exception to the employment-service criminal records check, item I). [AGENCY NAME] notifies ODA or its designee within 7 days of any change in the agency's telephone number, mailing address or email address. ODM also requires contact updates within 7 days and the agency makes them to ODM at the same time.
